title: ClinRx India-focused antibiotic profile collection
scope: Systemic, antimycobacterial and local-use antibiotics, with separate India-evidence and clinical-content coverage. Includes additional international reference candidates pending Indian availability verification.
coverage_limit: A broad working collection, not a certified list of all currently marketed Indian antibiotics, formulations or brands. Each clinical summary requires source reconciliation and clinical/pharmacy review. Supplemental evidence links were verified by the user on 28–29 October 2026; the clinical summaries remain drafts and require review.

records.name: Amikacin
forms: IV/IM amikacin sulfate; ophthalmic products require separate route-specific profiles

overview.text: Parenteral aminoglycoside with concentration-dependent antibacterial activity.

mechanism.text: Binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and disrupts bacterial protein synthesis.

spectrum.text: Susceptible aerobic Gram-negative bacilli, including selected resistant isolates; no activity against anaerobes. Susceptibility is local and isolate-specific.

indications.text: NCDC 2025 includes amikacin in selected urinary and severe-infection pathways; use only when the organism and site support it.

dosing.text:
For conventional treatment of susceptible serious infections, the US injection label recommends 15 mg/kg/day IV or IM, administered as 7.5 mg/kg every 12 hours or 5 mg/kg every 8 hours. The conventional adult maximum is 1.5 g/day. Children and older infants with normal renal function receive the same weight-based daily total. Dose and interval must be individualised using renal function and serum concentrations; neonatal dosing requires a separate protocol. US prescribing information.

For eligible adults, an institutional extended-interval strategy uses 15 mg/kg IV every 24 hours when creatinine clearance is ≥60 mL/min, with a timed concentration and the specified amikacin nomogram determining subsequent intervals. Conventional and extended-interval dosing require different concentration interpretation. Mycobacterial infections and patients excluded from the nomogram require indication-specific dosing. UCSF dosing guidance.

adjustments.text: Renal impairment requires individualized dose/interval planning; dialysis and rapidly changing renal function need a dedicated protocol.

pharmacokinetics.text: Poor oral absorption; distributes mainly in extracellular fluid and is eliminated largely unchanged by glomerular filtration.

pharmacodynamics.text: Concentration-dependent killing and a post-antibiotic effect are described; therapeutic drug monitoring is used in selected regimens.

safety.text: Boxed risks include nephrotoxicity, usually irreversible ototoxicity, neurotoxicity and neuromuscular blockade.

interactions.text: Additive toxicity with other nephrotoxic/ototoxic agents; neuromuscular blockers can increase paralysis risk.

populations.text: Pregnancy requires careful risk-benefit review; newborns, older adults and people with renal/hearing impairment need special oversight.

administration.text: IV infusion or IM administration only as specified by the exact formulation; avoid route/unit assumptions from topical products.

monitoring.text: Renal function, urine output, hearing/vestibular symptoms and serum concentrations when the protocol calls for them.

stewardship.text: Obtain cultures when feasible, narrow promptly, and avoid prolonged or duplicate aminoglycoside exposure.

records.name: Amoxicillin
forms: Oral capsules; referenced label also describes oral tablets and suspension.

overview.text: Orally absorbed aminopenicillin without a beta-lactamase inhibitor.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, producing bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms.

spectrum.text: Selected susceptible respiratory and urinary pathogens; beta-lactamase production can confer resistance.

indications.text: ENT, skin and genitourinary infections; H. pylori use requires the specified combination regimen.

dosing.text: Adults >40 kg with mild/moderate ENT infection, normal renal function: 500 mg orally every 12 hours or 250 mg every 8 hours.

adjustments.text: Adjust in severe renal impairment; consult the GFR/dialysis table. The 875-mg dose is unsuitable below GFR 30 mL/min.

pharmacokinetics.text: Rapid oral absorption; peak concentrations occur around 1–2 hours, with substantial renal elimination.

pharmacodynamics.text: Class-level PK/PD summary: beta-lactam activity is linked to the proportion of the dosing interval that unbound drug remains above the organism MIC (%fT>MIC). A 2020 critically-ill-adult position paper summarizes preclinical efficacy targets of about 60–70% fT>MIC for penicillins and clinical ICU targets often spanning roughly 45–100%, depending on subclass and study. These are population-level evidence summaries, not an individual dose target. The appropriate exposure depends on the organism/MIC, infection site, severity, renal clearance, regimen and toxicity risk; prolonged infusion or therapeutic drug monitoring is a protocol-level decision. No validated drug-specific bedside target for this medicine and every Indian indication was verified.

safety.text: Anaphylaxis, severe skin reactions and colitis; rash is frequent in infectious mononucleosis.

interactions.text: Allopurinol increases rash risk; probenecid increases exposure; monitor anticoagulation when applicable.

populations.text: Infants ≤12 weeks need a distinct schedule; pregnancy/lactation decisions require review.

administration.text: Measure liquid doses with a calibrated device; formulation concentration must be checked.

monitoring.text: Assess allergy, clinical response and renal function when impairment is possible.

stewardship.text: Use susceptibility results to reassess treatment; avoid use without a likely bacterial infection.

records.name: Amoxicillin–clavulanate
forms: Immediate-release oral tablets: amoxicillin/clavulanate 250/125, 500/125 or 875/125 mg.

overview.text: Clavulanate protects amoxicillin against selected beta-lactamases; formulations have different component ratios.

mechanism.text: Amoxicillin inhibits cell-wall synthesis; clavulanate inhibits susceptible beta-lactamases.

spectrum.text: Selected beta-lactamase-producing respiratory, skin and urinary pathogens; protection is not universal.

indications.text: Susceptible lower respiratory, sinus, ear, skin and urinary infections.

dosing.text:
Adults or patients ≥40 kg, mild/moderate labeled infection with normal renal function: 500/125 mg orally every 12 hours.

NTEP DR-TB regimen context (partial indication-specific addition): NTEP Table 3.7 specifies 875/125 mg orally twice daily in the longer oral M/XDR-TB regimen only as a companion to carbapenems. This is not a standalone infection dose; other indication-specific dosing and adjustments still require separate review.

adjustments.text: GFR <30 mL/min and dialysis require changes; do not use the 875-mg amoxicillin tablet in severe renal impairment.

pharmacokinetics.text: Both components are orally absorbed; renal clearance affects exposure.

pharmacodynamics.text: Class-level PK/PD summary: beta-lactam activity is linked to the proportion of the dosing interval that unbound drug remains above the organism MIC (%fT>MIC). A 2020 critically-ill-adult position paper summarizes preclinical efficacy targets of about 60–70% fT>MIC for penicillins and clinical ICU targets often spanning roughly 45–100%, depending on subclass and study. These are population-level evidence summaries, not an individual dose target. The appropriate exposure depends on the organism/MIC, infection site, severity, renal clearance, regimen and toxicity risk; prolonged infusion or therapeutic drug monitoring is a protocol-level decision. No validated drug-specific bedside target for this medicine and every Indian indication was verified. For a fixed combination, this class summary does not establish the exposure target of the inhibitor component.

safety.text: Prior combination-associated cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction contraindicates reuse; allergy and colitis also matter.

interactions.text: Review anticoagulants, allopurinol and probenecid.

populations.text: Pediatric doses depend on amoxicillin content and exact clavulanate ratio; separate tables are required.

administration.text: Take at the start of a meal. Two 250/125-mg tablets are not equivalent to one 500/125-mg tablet.

monitoring.text: Monitor hepatic function when clinically indicated and investigate persistent diarrhea.

stewardship.text: Use susceptibility results to reassess treatment; avoid use without a likely bacterial infection.

records.name: Azithromycin
forms: Oral tablets/suspension; IV infusion; ophthalmic products are separate route-specific formulations

overview.text: Azalide macrolide with oral and IV systemic products; do not transfer systemic doses to ophthalmic formulations.

mechanism.text: Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibits bacterial protein synthesis.

spectrum.text: Activity includes selected respiratory, atypical and sexually transmitted pathogens; resistance and syndrome matter.

indications.text: NCDC lists azithromycin in selected Indian respiratory and enteric-fever pathways; exact use depends on diagnosis, age and local susceptibility.

dosing.text:
For labelled mild community-acquired pneumonia in adults, administer 500 mg PO on day 1, followed by 250 mg once daily on days 2–5. Some other labelled indications use 500 mg once daily for 3 days; the indication must remain attached to the regimen. For community-acquired pneumonia in children aged ≥6 months, the labelled schedule is 10 mg/kg on day 1, followed by 5 mg/kg once daily on days 2–5, subject to the product’s weight-based maximum-dose tables. US prescribing information.

For uncomplicated chlamydial infection, 1 g PO once is an alternative regimen in nonpregnant adults and a recommended regimen during pregnancy. Treatment selection must follow current indication-specific guidance and local resistance patterns. CDC chlamydia guideline.

adjustments.text: No routine renal adjustment in mild/moderate impairment is stated in the cited label; severe renal or hepatic disease needs product-specific review.

pharmacokinetics.text: Extensive tissue distribution and long terminal elimination; predominantly biliary elimination.

pharmacodynamics.text: Animal infection models associate activity with AUC/MIC for selected pathogens; a clinical trial exposure-response target is not established in labeling.

safety.text: QT prolongation/torsades risk, hepatotoxicity, severe allergy and C. difficile-associated diarrhea are important concerns.

interactions.text: Review QT-prolonging medicines, warfarin/INR and drugs affecting cardiac rhythm; label-specific interactions should be checked.

populations.text: Pregnancy, lactation, infants and people with cardiac or hepatic risk need indication-specific review.

administration.text: Follow the selected formulation’s food, reconstitution and infusion directions; oral and IV forms are not automatically interchangeable by schedule.

monitoring.text: Clinical response, allergy, liver injury and ECG/electrolytes when cardiac risk warrants.

stewardship.text: Avoid treatment of likely viral syndromes and empiric use where local resistance makes activity unreliable.

records.name: Aztreonam
forms: AZACTAM aztreonam powder, 1 g or 2 g, for IV/IM use; inhaled lysine formulation excluded.

overview.text: Monocyclic beta-lactam with a restricted antibacterial spectrum.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis through penicillin-binding proteins.

spectrum.text: Aerobic Gram-negative bacteria including susceptible Pseudomonas; additional agents are needed for suspected Gram-positive/anaerobic infection.

indications.text: Selected urinary, lower respiratory, bloodstream, skin, gynecological and intra-abdominal Gram-negative infections.

dosing.text: Adult susceptible UTI, normal renal function: 500 mg–1 g IV or IM every 8–12 hours; maximum total dose 8 g/day.

adjustments.text: Reduce maintenance doses in renal impairment after a loading dose; consult severe-impairment and hemodialysis instructions.

pharmacokinetics.text: Elimination is largely renal; clearance falls with kidney impairment.

pharmacodynamics.text: Class-level PK/PD summary: beta-lactam activity is linked to the proportion of the dosing interval that unbound drug remains above the organism MIC (%fT>MIC). A 2020 critically-ill-adult position paper summarizes preclinical efficacy targets of about 60–70% fT>MIC for monobactams and clinical ICU targets often spanning roughly 45–100%, depending on subclass and study. These are population-level evidence summaries, not an individual dose target. The appropriate exposure depends on the organism/MIC, infection site, severity, renal clearance, regimen and toxicity risk; prolonged infusion or therapeutic drug monitoring is a protocol-level decision. No validated drug-specific bedside target for this medicine and every Indian indication was verified.

safety.text: Hypersensitivity, colitis, liver-test abnormalities and blood-count changes can occur; prior beta-lactam allergy still warrants assessment.

interactions.text: Do not assume IV admixture compatibility; consult product-specific compatibility data.

populations.text: Pediatric IV dosing with normal kidneys is described; pediatric IM and renal-impairment data are insufficient.

administration.text: Use IV for severe infection or doses >1 g; follow route-specific dilution instructions.

monitoring.text: Assess kidney function and blood counts/liver tests as clinically indicated.

stewardship.text: Use susceptibility results to reassess treatment; avoid use without a likely bacterial infection.

records.name: Bedaquiline
forms: Oral tablets containing bedaquiline as fumarate: 20 mg and 100 mg in inspected US label

overview.text: Key oral drug for resistant TB. Its long persistence and QT effects require coordinated companion-drug and safety review.

mechanism.text: Inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, impairing energy production.

spectrum.text: Susceptible M. tuberculosis including rifampicin-resistant strains; resistance can compromise newer all-oral regimens.

indications.text: Indian BPaLM and selected other DR-TB regimens, subject to eligibility.

dosing.text: India / NTEP regimen context only (not a standalone dose): eligible BPaLM patients aged ≥14 years receive 400 mg orally once daily in weeks 1–2, then 200 mg three times weekly in weeks 3–26; treatment may extend through week 39 under NTEP criteria. The 9–11-month and longer oral DR-TB regimens use different weight-band and duration rules. Regimen selection, resistance results, prior exposure and monitoring must be managed by an NTEP DR-TB centre.

adjustments.text: No US-label adjustment for mild/moderate renal or hepatic impairment; severe dysfunction requires caution and close adverse-event review.

pharmacokinetics.text: Food increases absorption; highly protein bound with prolonged terminal elimination and CYP3A metabolism.

pharmacodynamics.text: Bedaquiline exposure-response and toxicity relationships remain complex; the 2026 review concludes that no plasma, metabolite, AUC or MIC-normalized exposure target has been prospectively validated for routine dose adjustment. Standard regimen dosing should not be empirically altered from an isolated level; ensure combination-regimen integrity, food administration and ECG/electrolyte monitoring for QT risk.

safety.text: QT prolongation and hepatotoxicity are central hazards; ventricular arrhythmia or marked QT prolongation requires action.

interactions.text: Avoid moderate/strong CYP3A inducers. CYP3A inhibitors and other QT-prolonging drugs require safety review.

populations.text: US pediatric eligibility is age/weight limited; WHO/Indian programme use must follow their own pediatric tables and formulations.

administration.text: Take with food. Use the tablet-specific swallowing/dispersal instructions and supervised adherence support.

monitoring.text: Baseline/serial ECG, potassium, magnesium, calcium and liver assessment; reassess syncope or palpitations promptly.

stewardship.text: Never add alone to a failing TB regimen. Protect activity through susceptibility assessment and a reliably effective full combination.

records.name: Capreomycin
forms: Capreomycin disulfate powder for IM injection or IV infusion, 1 g activity in historical US label; historical Indian 750 mg vial specification

overview.text: Historical injectable TB drug retained for coverage auditing. An old product label does not establish a current recommended regimen or availability.

mechanism.text: Antimycobacterial polypeptide; a detailed molecular mechanism was not verified in the inspected prescribing information.

spectrum.text: Susceptible M. tuberculosis; potential cross-resistance with other injectable drugs requires specialist interpretation.

indications.text: Historical TB combination use; current all-oral NTEP guidance must govern regimen selection.

dosing.text: A current universal regimen dose is not provided here because WHO 2025 explicitly recommends that capreomycin not be included in longer MDR/RR-TB regimens. Do not use an old weight-based schedule as a default. Any exceptional/salvage use would require an expert TB programme decision, susceptibility context and a dedicated toxicity-monitoring protocol.

adjustments.text: Renal insufficiency increases exposure substantially; historical label supplies creatinine-clearance-based dose/interval tables.

pharmacokinetics.text: Poor oral absorption mandates parenteral delivery; renal elimination causes accumulation with impaired kidney function.

pharmacodynamics.text:
Capreomycin is a tuberactinomycin that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding at the ribosomal subunit interface, between helix 44 of 16S rRNA and helix 69 of 23S rRNA, interfering with translocation. Stanley et al., structural study.

TlyA-mediated rRNA methylation contributes to the binding environment; loss-of-function tlyA mutations can confer resistance. Primary TlyA–capreomycin structural study.

Unresolved evidence gap: A universally validated human capreomycin PK/PD efficacy target was not identified in the reviewed evidence. An aminoglycoside Cmax/MIC target should not be assumed to apply. Capreomycin is no longer recommended by WHO for MDR-TB regimens because of unfavourable outcomes and toxicity. WHO guidance.

The cited US label reports peak serum concentrations of approximately 28–32 µg/mL after 1 g intramuscularly in small studies and urinary excretion of about 52% within 12 hours in volunteers with normal renal function. These are descriptive pharmacokinetic observations, not an exposure–response target; concentrations were higher at 24 hours in two patients with marked renal impairment. Capreomycin label.

Clinical-outcome evidence: an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 12,030 people with MDR-TB found capreomycin performed no better than no injectable drug; among isolates susceptible to the compared injectable, amikacin was associated with more cures and fewer deaths than capreomycin. This supports the limited role reflected in current guidance; it does not establish a capreomycin exposure–response target. PMC-CAPREO-IPDMA-2021.

source_inclusion_approval.scope: Approval covers inclusion and citation of the listed references in the antibiotic module; it is not clinical validation or approval for treatment decisions.

safety.text: Nephrotoxicity, cochlear/vestibular toxicity, electrolyte loss and neuromuscular blockade are major hazards.

interactions.text: Concurrent aminoglycosides and other nephrotoxic/ototoxic medicines can compound potentially irreversible injury.

populations.text: Pregnancy safety is not established; the inspected US label does not establish pediatric safety/effectiveness.

administration.text: Historical label distinguishes IM injection from diluted IV infusion; no preparation protocol is encoded here.

monitoring.text: Monitor creatinine, urine findings, hearing/vestibular symptoms and potassium/magnesium if exceptional specialist use occurs.

stewardship.text: WHO 2025: capreomycin is not to be included in longer MDR/RR-TB regimens; contemporary care prioritizes all-oral regimens when possible. The current India DR-TB guideline/programme should determine any exceptional individualized regimen.

interactions.text:
When cefepime–zidebactam is coadministered with aminoglycosides, monitor renal function because of increased nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity potential. With potent diuretics such as furosemide, monitor renal function; this warning reflects cephalosporin experience. Cefepime may produce false-positive urine glucose results with certain methods; glucose-oxidase-based testing is recommended. ZAYNICH prescribing information, sections 7.1–7.3.

No drug interaction was observed among cefepime, zidebactam and metronidazole in the cited clinical study. In-vitro CYP and transporter findings suggest low interaction potential for zidebactam, but do not establish absence of all clinical interactions. Compatibility with other drugs in the same administration solution is unestablished and must be assessed separately. ZAYNICH prescribing information, sections 2.4 and 12.3.

records.name: Cefpirome
forms: Historical CEFROM cefpirome sulfate injection powder; HPRA licence withdrawn in 2001.

overview.text: Injectable cephalosporin with an exact-molecule entry in Bangladesh National Formulary 2019. Irish CEFROM registration is withdrawn; neither establishes Indian availability.

mechanism.text: Fourth-generation cephalosporin beta-lactam: inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins. The exact cefpirome-specific target-affinity detail was not separately verified in a current regulator label; class mechanism summary only.

spectrum.text: Formulary describes infections due to susceptible Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria; detailed current resistance limits remain unverified.

indications.text: Formulary includes complicated upper/lower UTI, skin/soft-tissue and respiratory infections, severe bacteremia/septicemia and neutropenic infections.

dosing.text: Formulary adult complicated UTI regimen: 1 g IV every 12 hours; very severe infection 2 g every 12 hours. Normal-renal context assumed; renal adjustment must be verified.

adjustments.text: A 1992 single-dose PK study proposed full maintenance dosing when CrCl >50 mL/min, 50% of usual daily dose at CrCl 20–50, and 25% below 20, with a 1 g initial dose; this is historical study-derived guidance, not a current India-approved dosing table. The Indonesian manufacturer Cefrin product information contains its own renal-impairment regimen. Verify the exact local product insert and dialysis protocol before use; accumulation can cause encephalopathy, myoclonus or seizures.

pharmacokinetics.text: Renally eliminated; the small single-dose PK study found cefpirome half-life increased from about 2 hours in healthy subjects to about 14.5 hours in uraemia, with reduced clearance. Renal function therefore materially changes exposure. This is an older study and does not establish current India dosing.

pharmacodynamics.text: Class-level PK/PD summary: beta-lactam activity is linked to the proportion of the dosing interval that unbound drug remains above the organism MIC (%fT>MIC). A 2020 critically-ill-adult position paper summarizes preclinical efficacy targets of about 60–70% fT>MIC for cephalosporins and clinical ICU targets often spanning roughly 45–100%, depending on subclass and study. These are population-level evidence summaries, not an individual dose target. The appropriate exposure depends on the organism/MIC, infection site, severity, renal clearance, regimen and toxicity risk; prolonged infusion or therapeutic drug monitoring is a protocol-level decision. No validated drug-specific bedside target for this medicine and every Indian indication was verified.

safety.text: The entry refers to cephalosporin/cefadroxil cautions: allergy/anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal effects and hepatic abnormalities. Exact-molecule current safety labeling remains missing.

interactions.text: Published cefpirome monograph advises close renal monitoring with high-dose aminoglycosides or potent diuretics such as furosemide because of nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity concerns; concomitant nephrotoxic agents warrant review. This is class/monograph evidence rather than contemporary India label text.

populations.text: Formulary does not recommend use below age 12; pregnancy, lactation and neonatal details require a current label.

administration.text: Formulary specifies IV injection or infusion; reconstitution, infusion duration and stability remain unverified.

monitoring.text: Monitor renal function and neurologic status, especially when CrCl ≤50 mL/min or renal function is changing; accumulation has been associated with encephalopathy, myoclonus and seizures. Check clinical/microbiological response and hypersensitivity. No current India-specific cefpirome monitoring protocol was found.

stewardship.text:
Cefpirome is classified WHO AWaRe Watch for antibiotic-use monitoring and has not been listed on the WHO Essential Medicines List. Watch classification does not itself establish a preferred indication. WHO cefpirome record.

Select cefpirome according to the infection, reliable susceptibility results, local epidemiology and available alternatives. Reassess empirical therapy as culture and clinical information become available; a 48–72-hour antibiotic review can support discontinuation, narrowing or other optimisation. This is a general stewardship intervention, not cefpirome-specific trial evidence. CDC hospital stewardship guidance.

Do not regard a favourable standard-inoculum MIC as proof of reliable activity against ESBL-producing organisms: primary research demonstrated an inoculum effect with cefpirome against SHV-ESBL-producing isolates. Primary cefpirome inoculum study.

Class-level context only: the 2025 IDSA complicated-UTI guideline includes third- or fourth-generation cephalosporins among options for selected patients without sepsis, while grading evidence for these classes as very low certainty. It does not name cefpirome; this cannot be used to infer cefpirome-specific efficacy or preferred status. IDSA 2025 cUTI guideline.

A PMC-hosted IDSA AMR guidance document advises avoiding cefepime for ESBL pyelonephritis/cUTI and invasive ESBL infection, while discussing no cefpirome regimen. This is a reason not to extrapolate cefepime stewardship recommendations to cefpirome; it is not direct cefpirome comparative evidence. IDSA AMR guidance.

Unresolved evidence gap: Modern direct evidence establishing a cefpirome-specific stewardship advantage or preferred role in AmpC/ESBL infection remains limited. Current cefepime recommendations cannot be assumed to apply to cefpirome. IDSA AMR guidance.

records.name: Chloramphenicol
forms: IV chloramphenicol sodium succinate; oral and ophthalmic formulations require separate source/route verification

overview.text: Broad-spectrum amphenicol; systemic use is constrained by serious hematologic toxicity.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 50S ribosomal subunit.

spectrum.text: Broad in-vitro activity is not a reliable predictor of current susceptibility; resistance varies by organism and region.

indications.text: NCDC mentions chloramphenicol in selected Indian discussions; confirm whether it is a current recommended option for the particular syndrome.

dosing.text:
For the cited US IV chloramphenicol sodium succinate formulation, the usual dose is 50 mg/kg/day divided into four doses every 6 hours. Exceptional severe infections may require up to 100 mg/kg/day, reduced to the usual dose as soon as clinically appropriate. Premature infants, neonates and children with immature metabolism generally receive 25 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours, with serum-concentration guidance. Full-term infants older than 2 weeks may receive up to 50 mg/kg/day under specialist supervision. This US formulation is intended for IV administration only.

Reserve chloramphenicol for serious susceptible infections when safer effective agents are unsuitable. Obtain baseline blood counts and repeat approximately every 2 days during treatment; normal blood counts do not exclude subsequent aplastic anaemia. Impaired elimination requires dose reassessment and preferably serum-concentration measurement.

adjustments.text: Hepatic metabolism, neonatal physiology and renal impairment affect exposure; use specialist/pharmacy review.

pharmacokinetics.text: IV sodium succinate is a prodrug formulation requiring conversion to active chloramphenicol; exposure varies with organ function.

pharmacodynamics.text:
Chloramphenicol inhibits protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal peptidyl-transferase centre. Experimental studies show that translation inhibition depends partly on the nascent peptide and incoming amino acid rather than uniformly blocking every peptide bond. Marks et al., 2016.

Activity is generally bacteriostatic. A major resistance mechanism is drug inactivation by chloramphenicol acetyltransferase. Primary resistance study.

A recent PK/PD review specifically reports that chloramphenicol pharmacodynamics have not been directly studied in animal or human models; its target-attainment analysis borrowed a florfenicol target from an ex-vivo pig-ileum model. This does not establish an efficacy target for chloramphenicol in patients. PMC review and modelling study.

Unresolved evidence gap: A universal, clinically validated human AUC/MIC or time-above-MIC target was not identified in the reviewed evidence. Serum-concentration monitoring used to individualise exposure and reduce toxicity should not be presented as a validated organism-specific efficacy target.

Adult consensus guidance recommends concentration monitoring for courses likely to exceed 48 hours and gives suggested peak/trough safety ranges. These monitoring ranges are intended to reduce toxicity; they do not define an organism-specific human efficacy target or a validated AUC/MIC threshold. Scottish Antimicrobial Prescribing Group consensus guidance.

source_inclusion_approval.scope: Approval covers inclusion and citation of the listed references in the antibiotic module; it is not clinical validation or approval for treatment decisions.

safety.text: Potentially fatal aplastic anemia, dose-related marrow suppression, gray baby syndrome and hypersensitivity are major hazards.

interactions.text: Review marrow-suppressive medicines and interactions affecting hepatic metabolism; exact product labeling is required.

populations.text: Avoid casual use in pregnancy/newborns; newborns and infants are especially vulnerable to accumulation and toxicity.

administration.text: IV route only for the cited product; reconstitute and administer exactly as its label specifies.

monitoring.text: CBC with differential/reticulocytes and hepatic/renal status during use; monitor for marrow and neonatal toxicity.

stewardship.text: Reserve systemic use for serious infections when safer effective alternatives are unsuitable and expert review supports it.

records.name: Ciprofloxacin
forms: Oral tablets/suspension; IV infusion; ophthalmic/otic preparations are separate products

overview.text: Fluoroquinolone with systemic and route-specific topical products.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.

spectrum.text: Selected Gram-negative pathogens including susceptible Pseudomonas; unreliable for many Gram-positive infections and resistance is significant.

indications.text: NCDC includes fluoroquinolones only in selected syndrome/context pathways and advises against some empirical uses; check the current Indian table.

dosing.text:
Adult labelled oral regimens include 250–500 mg every 12 hours for urinary tract infections and 500–750 mg every 12 hours for lower respiratory tract infections, with treatment duration determined by the infection and applicable guideline. Approximate exposure-equivalent regimens are 500 mg PO every 12 hours and 400 mg IV every 12 hours, or 750 mg PO every 12 hours and 400 mg IV every 8 hours. Conversion requires clinical assessment and adequate oral absorption. US prescribing information.

For labelled complicated UTI or pyelonephritis in children aged 1–17 years, administer 10–20 mg/kg PO every 12 hours, maximum 750 mg per dose; the label specifies 10–21 days. Renal impairment requires adjustment. These labelled regimens do not establish ciprofloxacin as preferred empirical therapy for every listed infection. US prescribing information: paediatric dosing.

adjustments.text: Renal elimination is substantial; adjust systemic dosing for kidney impairment using the specific product table.

pharmacokinetics.text: Orally absorbed and widely distributed; renal clearance and food/mineral interactions affect exposure.

pharmacodynamics.text: Fluoroquinolone activity relates to AUC/MIC and peak/MIC measures; use susceptibility interpretation, not the profile as a target calculator.

safety.text: Boxed/major risks include tendinitis and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects and exacerbation of myasthenia gravis; QT and dysglycemia risks also matter.

interactions.text: Separate oral dosing from polyvalent cations; review warfarin, QT-prolonging agents, theophylline and glucose-lowering medicines.

populations.text: Avoid or reserve in pregnancy and children except when a specific risk-benefit indication supports it.

administration.text: Oral, IV and topical products are not equivalent by dose; follow exact formulation guidance and avoid rapid IV administration.

monitoring.text: Renal function, neurological/tendon symptoms, glucose or ECG monitoring when patient-specific risk warrants.

stewardship.text: Reserve systemic fluoroquinolones for indications with expected benefit; obtain cultures where appropriate and de-escalate.

records.name: Ciprofloxacin — ophthalmic
forms: Sterile ciprofloxacin 0.3% ophthalmic solution; not an otic product

overview.text: Sterile ophthalmic fluoroquinolone; distinct from systemic and otic ciprofloxacin products.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.

spectrum.text: Label covers selected susceptible ocular Gram-negative and Gram-positive organisms; local isolate susceptibility matters.

indications.text: US label indications include bacterial conjunctivitis and corneal ulcer due to specified susceptible organisms.

dosing.text: For ciprofloxacin 0.3% ophthalmic solution, treat bacterial conjunctivitis with 1–2 drops into the affected eye every 2 hours while awake for 2 days, followed by 1–2 drops every 4 hours while awake for 5 days. For corneal ulcers, administer 2 drops every 15 minutes for the first 6 hours, then every 30 minutes for the remainder of day 1; administer 2 drops hourly on day 2, then every 4 hours on days 3–14. Treatment beyond 14 days depends on corneal re-epithelialisation and ophthalmic reassessment. These schedules apply to the solution; ointment requires its own instructions. Ophthalmic solution prescribing information.

adjustments.text: Low systemic exposure is expected from topical ophthalmic use; systemic renal dosing tables should not be transferred to eye drops.

pharmacokinetics.text: Topical ocular administration produces local exposure; some systemic absorption may occur.

pharmacodynamics.text: Topical eye treatment creates compartment-specific exposure: a human surgical sampling study found topical ciprofloxacin produced lower vitreous concentrations than oral dosing, despite similar aqueous levels under the study’s intensive instillation schedule. This was a penetration study, not an infection-outcome target study; do not infer a universal ophthalmic PK/PD target or use systemic dose logic for eye drops.

safety.text: Ocular discomfort, deposits, hypersensitivity and hypersensitivity to quinolones are relevant; severe systemic quinolone reactions have been reported.

interactions.text: Systemic interaction risk is expected to be limited but review concurrent eye products and hypersensitivity history.

populations.text: Pregnancy, lactation and pediatric restrictions depend on the indication and exact label; corneal ulcer care is specialist-led.

administration.text: For ocular use only; never inject into the eye. Contact lenses and bottle-tip contamination require attention.

monitoring.text: Monitor pain, vision, discharge and corneal response; lack of improvement or worsening requires reassessment.

stewardship.text: Avoid antibiotic drops for viral/red-eye syndromes; culture/severity assessment and specialist review for corneal ulcer.

records.name: Clindamycin
forms: Oral capsules/solution; IV infusion; topical and vaginal products require separate route-specific profiles

overview.text: Lincosamide antibacterial available in oral, parenteral and topical products.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial protein synthesis through binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit.

spectrum.text: Selected Gram-positive cocci and anaerobes; susceptibility varies and inducible resistance testing can matter.

indications.text: NCDC includes clindamycin in selected Indian skin/soft-tissue and anaerobic or resistant Gram-positive pathways.

dosing.text:
Adult oral capsule dosing is 150–300 mg every 6 hours for serious infections or 300–450 mg every 6 hours for more severe infections. Oral prescribing information.

Adult parenteral dosing is 600–1,200 mg/day for serious infections or 1,200–2,700 mg/day for more severe infections, divided into 2–4 doses. 900 mg IV every 8 hours falls within the latter range. Doses up to 4,800 mg/day IV have been used in life-threatening infections but are not routine dosing targets. Single IM doses should not exceed 600 mg. Injection prescribing information.

A contemporary paediatric institutional regimen is 10 mg/kg per dose IV or PO every 8 hours, with usual route-specific maximum doses and higher-dose exceptions determined by the infection. UCSF paediatric guidance.

adjustments.text: Routine renal dose modification is generally not necessary in the cited label; severe hepatic impairment and prolonged therapy need review.

pharmacokinetics.text: Oral absorption is nearly complete; food has little effect; distributes into tissues but CSF levels are limited.

pharmacodynamics.text: For lincosamides, PK/PD literature associates antibacterial effect with AUC/MIC. The cited review does not establish a universal human clindamycin target across syndromes, pathogens and infection sites; use susceptibility, clinical response and syndrome-specific dosing.

safety.text: Prominent boxed risk: potentially severe or fatal C. difficile-associated colitis; also rash and hepatic/blood-count abnormalities.

interactions.text: Neuromuscular blocking agents may have enhanced effect; review other concomitant antibiotics and full product labeling.

populations.text: Pregnancy/lactation and pediatric use should be assessed by exact indication and product; older adults need attention to colitis.

administration.text: Swallow oral capsules with adequate water; IV and topical products require their own preparation and route directions.

monitoring.text: Monitor for diarrhea/colitis during and after treatment; review liver tests and CBC when treatment is prolonged.

stewardship.text: Reserve for susceptible organisms and appropriate syndromes; avoid redundant anaerobic or Gram-positive coverage.

records.name: Clofazimine
forms: Oral 50 mg soft gelatin capsules in inspected US label; programme formulations require separate verification

overview.text: Lipophilic antimycobacterial used in leprosy MDT and selected resistant-TB combinations; prolonged tissue retention shapes adverse effects.

mechanism.text: Exact antimicrobial mechanism is incompletely defined in the inspected label.

spectrum.text: Susceptible M. leprae; TB use is regimen specific and should not be inferred from the US leprosy indication.

indications.text: Indian leprosy triple MDT and selected NTEP DR-TB regimens.

dosing.text:
India / NTEP DR-TB context: adult daily dose in the 9–11-month shorter oral and longer oral M/XDR-TB tables is 50 mg (16–29 kg), 100 mg (30–45 kg), 100 mg (46–70 kg), or 200 mg (>70 kg). This is a component of a complete resistance-guided regimen, not monotherapy; do not substitute the separate NLEP leprosy MDT schedule.

Separate India / NLEP leprosy MDT schedule (not TB): adults with PB disease receive 300 mg once monthly plus 50 mg daily for 6 months; adults with MB disease receive the same doses for 12 months. Children aged 10–14 years receive 150 mg monthly plus 50 mg on alternate days for 6 months (PB) or 12 months (MB). Children 20–40 kg or under 10 years receive 100 mg monthly plus 50 mg twice weekly for 6 or 12 months, respectively. NLEP says children under 40 kg require single formulations.

adjustments.text: US label permits usual dosing in mild/moderate renal impairment; severe renal or hepatic dysfunction requires caution and benefit-risk review.

pharmacokinetics.text: Variable oral absorption; deposits in fatty and reticuloendothelial tissues and clears very slowly.

pharmacodynamics.text: In a prospective RR/MDR-TB cohort, clofazimine AUC0–24/MIC around 50.5 was associated with faster sputum culture conversion. This is observational regimen-level evidence, not a prospectively validated universal target or dose-escalation threshold; MIC method, companion drugs and susceptibility matter. Do not adjust standard NTEP dosing from this number alone.

safety.text: Brown-black skin/body-fluid discoloration, ichthyosis, severe intestinal deposition and QT prolongation can occur.

interactions.text: Other QT-prolonging medicines, including bedaquiline, may add risk; assess CYP3A substrate interactions.

populations.text: Counsel about persistent discoloration and possible psychological distress. Pregnancy/lactation require individual review.

administration.text: Administer orally with meals according to the programme regimen; do not import legacy US leprosy durations.

monitoring.text: Monitor abdominal pain, bowel symptoms, ECG when indicated and mood; investigate syncope and severe gastrointestinal symptoms.

stewardship.text: Use in an effective multidrug regimen; explain expected discoloration early to support adherence without minimizing serious toxicity.

records.name: Cloxacillin
forms: Oral cloxacillin sodium capsules and granules for solution.

overview.text: Penicillinase-resistant antistaphylococcal penicillin; the inspected Canadian monograph concerns oral products.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, producing bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms.

spectrum.text: Susceptible penicillinase-producing staphylococci and associated streptococci; susceptibility confirmation matters.

indications.text: Staphylococcal infections susceptible to cloxacillin, with or without accompanying streptococci.

dosing.text: Adults with mild/moderate susceptible infection, normal renal context: 250–500 mg orally every 6 hours; labeled daily ceiling 6 g.

adjustments.text: The cited product monograph cautions that high-dose cloxacillin in renal impairment may increase neurotoxicity risk and can contribute to electrolyte disturbance/volume-related complications; it does not provide a validated creatinine-clearance dosing table. Individualize high-dose therapy with renal, fluid/electrolyte and clinical monitoring, using the exact local product information.

pharmacokinetics.text: Rapid but incomplete oral absorption; fasting capsule and liquid exposures differ, so formulations need separate verification.

pharmacodynamics.text: Class-level PK/PD summary: beta-lactam activity is linked to the proportion of the dosing interval that unbound drug remains above the organism MIC (%fT>MIC). A 2020 critically-ill-adult position paper summarizes preclinical efficacy targets of about 60–70% fT>MIC for penicillins and clinical ICU targets often spanning roughly 45–100%, depending on subclass and study. These are population-level evidence summaries, not an individual dose target. The appropriate exposure depends on the organism/MIC, infection site, severity, renal clearance, regimen and toxicity risk; prolonged infusion or therapeutic drug monitoring is a protocol-level decision. No validated drug-specific bedside target for this medicine and every Indian indication was verified.

safety.text: Severe beta-lactam hypersensitivity is a contraindication; allergic reactions and neurotoxicity can occur.

interactions.text: Published product monograph lists possible interactions with probenecid (may increase penicillin concentrations), methotrexate (may increase exposure), mycophenolate (may reduce active metabolite exposure), warfarin (monitor INR), tetracyclines (possible antagonism) and live attenuated Ty21a typhoid vaccine (avoid concurrent use). These data are not an India-specific label; reconcile with current local product information and patient medicines.

populations.text: Pediatric schedules are weight-dependent; pregnancy/neonatal decisions require additional review.

administration.text: Give 1–2 hours before meals because food reduces absorption.

monitoring.text: Review clinical response and allergy; renal impairment can increase neurotoxicity risk.

stewardship.text: The monograph directs changing treatment when cultures do not confirm a susceptible staphylococcal pathogen.

records.name: Colistimethate sodium (colistin prodrug)
forms: Parenteral colistimethate sodium; unit expression varies by product

overview.text: Prodrug of colistin; not interchangeable with polymyxin B.

mechanism.text: Active colistin disrupts susceptible bacterial membranes.

spectrum.text: Selected aerobic Gram-negative bacteria; many organisms are intrinsically resistant.

indications.text: Severe susceptible Gram-negative infections when suitable alternatives are lacking.

dosing.text:
For adult IV treatment, the international polymyxin consensus recommends a loading dose of 300 mg colistin base activity (CBA), approximately 9 million IU, infused over 30–60 minutes, followed by the first maintenance dose 12–24 hours later. For normal renal function, recommended maintenance dosing is 300–360 mg CBA/day, divided every 12 hours. Renal impairment and renal replacement therapy require the guideline’s specific dosing tables. International polymyxin consensus, 2019.

Unit safety: approximately 1 million IU = 33 mg CBA = 80 mg chemical colistimethate sodium. Prescriptions must explicitly identify IU or mg CBA; mg CBA and mg chemical colistimethate are not interchangeable. International polymyxin consensus.

Exposure is highly variable. The operational plasma colistin target of approximately 2 mg/L may be insufficient for pulmonary infection and overlaps concentrations associated with nephrotoxicity. Nation et al., human dosing study.

adjustments.text: Dose and interval depend on kidney function and dialysis; use a dedicated protocol.

pharmacokinetics.text: Prodrug conversion and renal handling complicate prediction of active-colistin exposure.

pharmacodynamics.text:
Colistimethate sodium is a prodrug converted to active colistin. Antibacterial exposure depends on formed-colistin concentrations, with substantial variability in conversion and renal handling. Nation et al., human population-PK study.

Colistin interacts with bacterial lipopolysaccharide/lipid A and disrupts Gram-negative bacterial membranes. Primary colistin–LPS study.

In murine infection models, unbound AUC/MIC correlated best with activity. Required exposures varied by organism, strain and infection site, with poorer activity against pulmonary infection in relevant models. Dudhani et al., 2010; primary thigh/lung study, 2015.

A 2025 systematic review of 60 adult PK studies found substantial clinical PK variability; creatinine clearance was commonly reported as a covariate affecting CMS/colistin clearance. This supports separating dose/exposure monitoring from efficacy-target claims. PMC systematic review.

Human translation: international consensus guidance proposes a total plasma Css,avg near 2 mg/L (AUCss,24 about 50 mg·h/L) as a practical upper exposure target for colistin, based on preclinical efficacy translation and clinical nephrotoxicity data. It explicitly treats this as a maximum tolerable exposure, potentially inadequate for pneumonia; concentrations above it increase AKI risk. This is not a prospectively validated human efficacy threshold. International polymyxin consensus.

Unresolved evidence gap: Experimental targets are not universally validated human efficacy thresholds. Any numerical target must identify whether it describes animal-model efficacy, a human operational exposure target or toxicity risk.

Clinical safety context: a meta-analysis of five RCTs (377 participants, mostly critically ill adults) found nephrotoxicity in 36.2% of colistin recipients and higher risk than beta-lactam comparators (RR 2.40; 95% CI 1.47–3.91; NNH 5). The trials did not correlate toxicity with a specific exposure; this supports careful risk-benefit and renal monitoring, not a new efficacy target or dose algorithm. PMC-COLISTIN-RCT-META-2021.

populations.text: Pregnancy and pediatric use require specialist benefit–risk assessment.

administration.text: Verify vial strength and units at preparation, ordering and administration.

monitoring.text: Renal function, urine output, neurological symptoms and respiratory status.

stewardship.text: Reserve for a documented resistant-organism context; assess safer active alternatives.

records.name: Cycloserine
forms: Oral 250 mg capsules in inspected Seromycin label

overview.text: Oral second-line TB drug with a narrow margin between useful exposure and neurological toxicity. Renal clearance is clinically important.

mechanism.text: Inhibits cell-wall synthesis in susceptible bacteria.

spectrum.text: M. tuberculosis susceptible to cycloserine; non-TB label activity does not support routine empirical use.

indications.text: Active pulmonary/extrapulmonary TB when primary therapy is inadequate, always with other effective medicines.

dosing.text: India / NTEP longer oral M/XDR-TB context: adult daily dose is 250 mg (16–29 kg), 500 mg (30–45 kg), 750 mg (46–70 kg), or 1,000 mg (>70 kg); the NTEP table allows divided dosing for intolerance. Use only as part of a specialist-designed regimen; pyridoxine is specified by regimen/weight band.

adjustments.text: Severe renal insufficiency is contraindicated in the inspected US label; specialist adjustment and concentration monitoring are needed with impaired clearance.

pharmacokinetics.text: Readily absorbed orally, penetrates CSF, and is largely eliminated renally; excess levels increase toxicity.

pharmacodynamics.text: An HFS-TB model reported %T>MIC of 30% for cycloserine. These are translational model-derived exposure targets, not prospectively validated bedside dose-adjustment rules; interpretation depends on MIC method, regimen, patient exposure and site of disease. Do not use alone to alter NTEP/DR-TB therapy.

safety.text: Seizures, depression, psychosis, confusion and other CNS effects can require withdrawal. Epilepsy and serious psychiatric illness are contraindications.

interactions.text: Alcohol increases seizure risk; ethionamide and isoniazid may increase CNS adverse effects.

populations.text: Pregnancy and breastfeeding require expert review because drug reaches fetal blood and milk; baseline psychiatric assessment is essential.

administration.text: Administer capsules within the selected regimen; pyridoxine support must follow the treating programme.

monitoring.text: Monitor mood, cognition, seizure symptoms and renal function; consider therapeutic drug monitoring where available.

stewardship.text: Keep reliable adherence support and prompt adverse-event access; unexplained behavioral change should not be dismissed during prolonged TB treatment.

records.name: Dapsone
forms: Oral 25 mg and 100 mg tablets in inspected label; topical acne gels require separate profiles

overview.text: Oral sulfone principally represented here for leprosy MDT. Topical acne products and noninfectious uses cannot share this dosing record.

mechanism.text: The label describes inhibition of susceptible M. leprae; detailed folate-target pharmacology was not independently verified for this draft.

spectrum.text: Susceptible M. leprae; other clinical contexts require their own indication-specific evidence.

indications.text: NLEP triple MDT includes dapsone for both PB and MB leprosy from April 2025.

dosing.text: NLEP revised MDT schedule: adults receive dapsone 100 mg orally daily as part of multidrug therapy (with rifampicin and clofazimine schedules according to the classification regimen). Children require weight/age-band dosing, and regimen choice/duration must follow NLEP; this is never dapsone monotherapy. The referenced table does not cover every weight/clinical subgroup.

adjustments.text:
Renal impairment: Oxford University Hospitals guidance recommends no routine dose adjustment; its monograph notes that dapsone is dialysed by HDF/high-flux haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis, yet lists the usual dose for these modalities. It advises caution and adverse-effect monitoring when GFR is <20 mL/min. This is institutional renal-dosing guidance; follow local dialysis timing policy. OUH dapsone monograph.

Hepatic impairment: The cited UK SmPC advises dose reduction in elderly patients with impaired hepatic function but provides no numerical reduction schedule. Severe anaemia and severe G6PD deficiency are contraindications in that SmPC; regular blood-count monitoring is recommended. UK SmPC.

For Pneumocystis treatment or prophylaxis in people with HIV, test G6PD before use and select another agent if deficiency is present. NIH Pneumocystis guideline.

A PMC case report and literature review describes dapsone-associated hemolysis in renal dysfunction despite normal G6PD and proposes hemoglobin monitoring after initiation in patients with renal dysfunction. This is a safety-monitoring signal, not evidence for a numerical dose reduction. PMC case report/review.

A PMC review recommends baseline and periodic CBC, liver and renal testing and notes that hepatic laboratory abnormalities may prompt dose reduction or discontinuation while the cause is evaluated. Its monitoring intervals are review-level suggestions and do not constitute a validated hepatic dose algorithm; institutional schedules vary. PMC review.

Unresolved evidence gap: A validated numerical hepatic-impairment or Child–Pugh-based dose-adjustment algorithm was not identified.

Safety evidence relevant to monitoring, not dose adjustment: a single-centre Indian retrospective leprosy cohort of 36 patients found a significant mean haemoglobin fall and classified 25% as dapsone-associated haemolysis; the authors support haematological testing, including a repeat value around one month. The small hospital-based sample does not estimate population risk. A separate case report describes severe hemolysis and recommends checking G6PD and weekly haemoglobin during the first month, but a single case cannot establish a universal schedule. Neither source provides a validated hepatic dose algorithm. PMC-DAPSONE-LEPROSY-HEMOLYSIS-INDIA-2024; PMC-DAPSONE-HEINZ-CASE-2025.

source_inclusion_approval.scope: Approval covers inclusion and citation of the listed references in the antibiotic module; it is not clinical validation or approval for treatment decisions.

pharmacokinetics.text: Orally absorbed with a long variable half-life; drug reaches breast milk in clinically relevant amounts.

pharmacodynamics.text: Both static and cidal activity against M. leprae is described; no clinical exposure target is supplied.

safety.text: Hemolysis and methemoglobinemia can occur without G6PD deficiency and are worse with deficiency; agranulocytosis and severe rash also occur.

interactions.text: Rifampicin lowers dapsone exposure; folate antagonists and other oxidant drugs can increase toxicity concerns.

populations.text: G6PD status, baseline anemia and cardiorespiratory reserve affect risk; neonatal hemolysis through breast milk is relevant.

administration.text: Give oral tablets as the prescribed MDT component; do not replace with topical gel.

monitoring.text: Monitor CBC/hemoglobin and hepatic symptoms; assess cyanosis, dyspnea, rash or fever. HbA1c may be falsely low.

stewardship.text: Leprosy needs complete MDT and reaction/nerve assessment; dapsone monotherapy promotes resistance and does not treat leprosy reactions adequately.

records.name: Delamanid
forms: Oral 50 mg film-coated tablets; EMA also describes 25 mg dispersible tablets for selected pediatric weights

overview.text: Newer TB medicine used with effective companions when regimen construction requires it. Pediatric formulations and eligibility differ between jurisdictions.

mechanism.text: Inhibits production of methoxy- and keto-mycolic acids needed for the mycobacterial cell wall.

spectrum.text: M. tuberculosis susceptible to delamanid; resistance and previous exposure influence suitability.

indications.text: EMA describes combination treatment of resistant pulmonary TB when standard medicines are unsuitable; Indian selection follows NTEP.

dosing.text: India / NTEP longer oral M/XDR-TB context: NTEP Table 3.7 lists 50 mg orally twice daily for 24 weeks for ages 6–11 years, and 100 mg twice daily for 24 weeks for age ≥12 years. This is a regimen component; verify age, formulation, eligibility and the full DR-TB regimen with the NTEP DR-TB centre.

adjustments.text: No adjustment for mild/moderate renal impairment in the inspected source; severe renal and hepatic dysfunction require specialist review.

pharmacokinetics.text: Highly protein bound; albumin-mediated metabolism contributes substantially. A metabolite contributes to QT prolongation.

pharmacodynamics.text: An HFS-TB model reported an AUC0–24/MIC index of 195 for delamanid. These are translational model-derived exposure targets, not prospectively validated bedside dose-adjustment rules; interpretation depends on MIC method, regimen, patient exposure and site of disease. Do not use alone to alter NTEP/DR-TB therapy.

safety.text: QT prolongation is the main specific hazard; low albumin and electrolyte disturbances can increase risk.

interactions.text: Strong CYP3A induction and additive QT effects require review; fluoroquinolones may intensify QT concerns.

populations.text: EMA currently includes infants/children from 10 kg, but this is not an Indian eligibility or availability statement.

administration.text: Take the prescribed formulation with food and effective companion TB medicines.

monitoring.text: Monitor ECG, electrolytes, albumin and hepatic function; investigate syncope or palpitations urgently.

stewardship.text: Use through specialist regimen design and active safety monitoring; never convert source-label eligibility into automatic treatment authorization.

records.name: Dicloxacillin
forms: Oral dicloxacillin sodium capsules, 250 mg or 500 mg.

overview.text: Oral antistaphylococcal penicillin; serious life-threatening infections need initial parenteral therapy.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, producing bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms.

spectrum.text: Targets susceptible penicillinase-producing staphylococci; resistance results require a treatment change.

indications.text: Susceptible staphylococcal infections of appropriate severity for oral therapy.

dosing.text: Adults with mild/moderate labeled infection, normal renal context: 125 mg orally every 6 hours; severe-infection label dose 250 mg every 6 hours.

adjustments.text: Consider dose reduction and concentration monitoring if renal impairment develops; no complete dialysis schedule is supplied.

pharmacokinetics.text: Absorption is incomplete; peak concentrations occur near 1–1.5 hours and meals delay absorption.

pharmacodynamics.text: Class-level PK/PD summary: beta-lactam activity is linked to the proportion of the dosing interval that unbound drug remains above the organism MIC (%fT>MIC). A 2020 critically-ill-adult position paper summarizes preclinical efficacy targets of about 60–70% fT>MIC for penicillins and clinical ICU targets often spanning roughly 45–100%, depending on subclass and study. These are population-level evidence summaries, not an individual dose target. The appropriate exposure depends on the organism/MIC, infection site, severity, renal clearance, regimen and toxicity risk; prolonged infusion or therapeutic drug monitoring is a protocol-level decision. No validated drug-specific bedside target for this medicine and every Indian indication was verified.

safety.text: Allergy, colitis, blood-count abnormalities and esophageal injury are relevant.

interactions.text: May reduce warfarin anticoagulation; probenecid prolongs exposure.

populations.text: Neonatal experience is limited; the label does not recommend a newborn dose.

administration.text: Take fasting with adequate water while upright; avoid immediately before bed.

monitoring.text: Periodically assess blood counts, renal indices and liver enzymes during therapy.

stewardship.text: Use susceptibility results to reassess treatment; avoid use without a likely bacterial infection.

overview.text: IV carbapenem; historical US label requires current local-label confirmation.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, producing bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms.

spectrum.text: Selected susceptible Gram-negative organisms including Pseudomonas, plus some Gram-positive organisms and anaerobes.

indications.text: Complicated intra-abdominal and urinary infections, including pyelonephritis; pneumonia is not a US-approved indication.

dosing.text: Adults ≥18 years with complicated UTI, creatinine clearance >50 mL/min: 500 mg IV over one hour every 8 hours for 10 days; concurrent bacteremia may require longer.

adjustments.text: Use reduced regimens for creatinine clearance ≤50 mL/min; dialysis evidence remains insufficient.

pharmacokinetics.text: Primarily renal clearance; renal impairment substantially increases exposure.

pharmacodynamics.text: Free-drug time above MIC correlates with effect in preclinical models; no universal bedside target is inferred.

safety.text: Allergy, seizures and colitis are risks; later FDA action added increased mortality in ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia.

interactions.text: Valproate levels fall; probenecid increases exposure.

populations.text: Pediatric efficacy/safety were not established in the inspected label.

administration.text: Reconstituted vial suspension requires further dilution; never administer directly.

monitoring.text: Assess kidney function and neurologic status.

stewardship.text: Use only for a supported susceptible infection and verify current local authorization.

records.name: Doxycycline
forms: Oral hyclate or monohydrate tablets/capsules; IV products vary; salts and release forms are not interchangeable by tablet count

overview.text: Tetracycline-class antibacterial available in multiple salts and release forms.

mechanism.text: Inhibits protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit; usually bacteriostatic.

spectrum.text: Activity includes selected atypical organisms, rickettsiae and susceptible Gram-positive/negative bacteria; tetracycline cross-resistance is common.

indications.text: NCDC includes doxycycline in selected Indian respiratory, zoonotic and sexually transmitted infection pathways; confirm syndrome-specific recommendations.

dosing.text:
The general adult oral label recommends 100 mg every 12 hours on day 1, followed by 100 mg/day; more severe infections require 100 mg every 12 hours throughout treatment. US prescribing information.

For uncomplicated chlamydial infection in nonpregnant adults and adolescents, administer 100 mg PO twice daily for 7 days. CDC chlamydia guideline.

For suspected tickborne rickettsial infection, administer 100 mg PO or IV twice daily in adults, or 2.2 mg/kg per dose twice daily in children weighing <45 kg, maximum 100 mg per dose. Continue for at least 3 days after fever resolves and clinical improvement is evident, with a minimum course of 5–7 days for the indications specified by CDC. Short-course treatment is recommended at all ages when indicated for rickettsial disease. CDC rickettsial treatment guidance.

adjustments.text: Usually no adjustment is required for renal impairment with doxycycline, but hepatic dysfunction, prolonged courses and product-specific advice still require review.

pharmacokinetics.text: Orally well absorbed; distributes widely, concentrates in bile and has a prolonged half-life relative to older tetracyclines.

pharmacodynamics.text: For tetracyclines, efficacy is associated with drug exposure relative to MIC (AUC/MIC); the exact target varies by drug, pathogen, site and model, and a validated universal human doxycycline target was not established by the cited review. This is a mechanistic class-level summary, not a dose calculator.

safety.text: Esophagitis, photosensitivity, gastrointestinal effects, intracranial hypertension and severe skin reactions can occur.

interactions.text: Iron, calcium, magnesium and aluminum products can reduce absorption; enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants may reduce exposure; review anticoagulants.

populations.text: Tooth/bone effects underpin caution during pregnancy and in young children; exceptions are disease- and guideline-specific and require clinician review.

administration.text: Take with adequate water and remain upright; separate from polyvalent cations according to product instructions.

monitoring.text: Clinical response, swallowing/esophageal symptoms, photosensitivity and hepatic effects during longer courses.

stewardship.text: Use only for a susceptible pathogen/syndrome; check local resistance and avoid duplicate tetracycline therapy.

records.name: Ertapenem
forms: Ertapenem sodium 1-g powder for IV or IM use; route-specific preparation differs.

overview.text: Longer-persistence carbapenem allowing once-daily adult dosing.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, producing bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms.

spectrum.text: Selected Enterobacterales, Gram-positive organisms and anaerobes; do not assume Pseudomonas or enterococcal coverage.

indications.text: Complicated intra-abdominal/urinary/skin infections, pneumonia, pelvic infection and colorectal surgical prophylaxis.

dosing.text: Adult complicated UTI, normal renal function: 1 g IV or IM every 24 hours; labeled total course 10–14 days may include appropriate oral step-down.

adjustments.text: Reduce at creatinine clearance ≤30 mL/min/1.73 m²; hemodialysis supplementation depends on timing.

pharmacokinetics.text: High concentration-dependent protein binding; adult half-life approximately four hours, with renal elimination.

pharmacodynamics.text: Class-level PK/PD summary: beta-lactam activity is linked to the proportion of the dosing interval that unbound drug remains above the organism MIC (%fT>MIC). A 2020 critically-ill-adult position paper summarizes preclinical efficacy targets of about 60–70% fT>MIC for carbapenems / penems and clinical ICU targets often spanning roughly 45–100%, depending on subclass and study. These are population-level evidence summaries, not an individual dose target. The appropriate exposure depends on the organism/MIC, infection site, severity, renal clearance, regimen and toxicity risk; prolonged infusion or therapeutic drug monitoring is a protocol-level decision. No validated drug-specific bedside target for this medicine and every Indian indication was verified.

safety.text: Seizures, allergy, colitis and infusion/injection-site reactions are relevant.

interactions.text: Valproate concentrations may fall substantially; probenecid increases exposure.

populations.text: Pediatric dosing differs below age 13; treatment evidence starts at three months.

administration.text: IV infusion over 30 minutes; IM preparation uses lidocaine and must never be injected IV.

monitoring.text: Review renal function, seizure history and clinical response.

stewardship.text: Use susceptibility results to reassess treatment; avoid use without a likely bacterial infection.

records.name: Erythromycin
forms: Oral base, stearate, estolate or ethylsuccinate products; salt/formulation affects use

overview.text: Macrolide antibacterial; multiple salts and release forms are not automatically interchangeable.

mechanism.text: Binds 50S ribosomal subunits and inhibits protein synthesis.

spectrum.text: Selected susceptible Gram-positive and respiratory pathogens; resistance may emerge and cross-resistance occurs.

indications.text: NCDC includes erythromycin in selected Indian respiratory and other syndrome contexts; verify present-day local recommendations.

dosing.text:
For the cited oral erythromycin base tablets, usual adult dosing is 250 mg four times daily or 500 mg every 12 hours. More severe infections may require up to 4 g/day, administered in more frequent divided doses; twice-daily administration is not recommended when the total daily dose exceeds 1 g. Usual paediatric dosing is 30–50 mg/kg/day in divided doses, with severe-infection increases subject to a 4 g/day maximum. The label specifies at least 10 days for streptococcal upper respiratory tract infection. US erythromycin base prescribing information.

Dosing and administration instructions are formulation-specific; base tablets, ethylsuccinate, estolate and IV lactobionate should not share an undifferentiated dosing field.

adjustments.text: Hepatic dysfunction and interacting medicines need review; hemodialysis does not remove erythromycin according to the inspected label.

pharmacokinetics.text: Oral absorption varies by patient and salt; drug concentrates in liver and is mainly excreted into bile.

pharmacodynamics.text: For macrolides such as erythromycin, PK/PD literature associates efficacy with exposure relative to MIC (AUC/MIC). The source is a class-level TDM review, not an erythromycin-specific validated clinical target; use infection-specific susceptibility and regimen guidance.

safety.text: GI intolerance, cholestatic/hepatic injury, QT prolongation and hearing effects can occur.

interactions.text: CYP3A-mediated interactions can be clinically important; review statins, anticoagulants and QT-prolonging drugs against current product labeling.

populations.text: Pregnancy, lactation, hepatic disease and congenital/acquired QT risk need assessment.

administration.text: Follow salt-specific food instructions and release-form handling; do not crush delayed-release tablets unless the exact label permits.

monitoring.text: Clinical response, hepatic symptoms, ECG/electrolytes for cardiac-risk patients and interacting-drug effects.

stewardship.text: Prefer pathogen-directed use where appropriate; consider resistance and avoid combination choices with antagonism concerns.

records.name: Ethambutol
forms: Oral ethambutol hydrochloride 100 mg and 400 mg tablets in inspected label

overview.text: Oral companion TB drug requiring careful vision assessment and renal review. International label age restrictions differ from programme practice.

mechanism.text: The inspected label describes impaired mycobacterial metabolism and multiplication; a detailed molecular target is not encoded.

spectrum.text: Susceptible M. tuberculosis; resistance can arise during inadequate combination treatment.

indications.text: Active pulmonary TB as part of effective multidrug therapy; it must not be used alone.

dosing.text: India / NTEP context: adult DS-TB uses daily HRZE for 2 months followed by HRE for 4 months, with fixed-dose combinations selected by weight band. The national workflow lists ethambutol 15 mg/kg daily (usual range 12–18 mg/kg) for adults. In adult DR-TB tables, the daily weight-band dose is 400 mg (16–29 kg), 800 mg (30–45 kg), 1,200 mg (46–70 kg), or 1,600 mg (>70 kg). These schedules are regimen-specific; use current pediatric tables and monitor vision/renal function.

adjustments.text: For stage IV–V CKD or haemodialysis, an ISCCM India position statement cites ethambutol 15–25 mg/kg three times weekly. This differs from routine daily NTEP weight-band therapy and requires specialist selection, dialysis timing and visual-acuity/colour-vision monitoring.

pharmacokinetics.text: Absorbed orally and substantially excreted unchanged in urine; impaired renal function increases exposure.

pharmacodynamics.text: A hollow-fiber system model of tuberculosis (HFS-TB) reported a Cmax/MIC index >0.51 for ethambutol. These are translational model-derived exposure targets, not prospectively validated bedside dose-adjustment rules; interpretation depends on MIC method, regimen, patient exposure and site of disease. Do not use alone to alter NTEP/DR-TB therapy.

safety.text: Optic neuropathy can impair acuity and red-green discrimination and may be irreversible. Hyperuricemia and hypersensitivity also occur.

interactions.text: Aluminium-containing antacids may reduce absorption; check administration separation in the product instructions.

populations.text: Children need an age-appropriate vision-monitoring strategy under current TB guidance; older patients often require renal reassessment.

administration.text: Oral administration is possible with food. Provide clear instructions to report visual changes immediately.

monitoring.text: Baseline and serial visual acuity/color assessment, symptom review and renal function are central safety checks.

stewardship.text: Preserve effective companion drugs; do not retain ethambutol blindly when resistance or ocular toxicity changes the benefit-risk balance.

records.name: Ethionamide
forms: Oral 250 mg film-coated tablets in inspected Trecator label

overview.text: Reserve oral TB medicine whose tolerability and resistance profile affect regimen selection. Modern programme alternatives must be reviewed first.

mechanism.text: Inhibits mycolic-acid synthesis after activation; cell-wall synthesis is disrupted.

spectrum.text: Susceptible M. tuberculosis; do not infer activity when relevant resistance mechanisms are present.

indications.text: Combined treatment when primary TB drugs are inadequate; current Indian regimen selection is programme directed.

dosing.text: India / NTEP DR-TB context: adult daily dose in the 9–11-month shorter oral regimen table is 375 mg (16–29 kg), 500 mg (30–45 kg), 750 mg (46–70 kg), or 1,000 mg (>70 kg) when ethionamide is selected; the longer oral M/XDR-TB table lists the same bands. The current shorter-regimen pathway generally uses linezolid in place of ethionamide. Use only when selected by the DR-TB team; the table permits divided doses for intolerance.

adjustments.text: Severe hepatic impairment is a contraindication in the inspected label; no validated renal/dialysis dosing rule is encoded here.

pharmacokinetics.text: Well absorbed orally, widely distributed including CSF, and extensively metabolized; formulation changes can alter peak concentrations.

pharmacodynamics.text: An HFS-TB model reported an AUC0–24/MIC index >56.2 for ethionamide. These are translational model-derived exposure targets, not prospectively validated bedside dose-adjustment rules; interpretation depends on MIC method, regimen, patient exposure and site of disease. Do not use alone to alter NTEP/DR-TB therapy.

safety.text: Gastrointestinal intolerance, hepatotoxicity, hypothyroidism, hypoglycemia and neurological effects can limit therapy.

interactions.text: Cycloserine can increase neurotoxicity; excessive alcohol may provoke psychiatric effects. Review other hepatotoxic drugs.

populations.text: Pregnancy and pediatric use require specialist benefit-risk assessment; diabetes increases the importance of glucose monitoring.

administration.text: Meals may improve tolerance. Dose escalation or divided administration must remain consistent with the chosen regimen.

monitoring.text: Check liver tests, thyroid function and glucose; evaluate vision changes and neuropsychiatric symptoms promptly.

stewardship.text: Use only within a susceptible effective regimen; do not substitute for another thioamide without accounting for cross-resistance.
