records.name: Faropenem
forms: Faropenem sodium immediate-release oral tablets; extended-release and medoxomil schedules excluded.

overview.text: Oral penem; sodium and medoxomil products must not be conflated.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, producing bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms.

spectrum.text: Legacy non-Indian in-vitro studies found activity against several streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, selected Enterobacterales and anaerobes. Activity was weak against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and poor against Enterococcus faecium; results vary by species and resistance phenotype. These historical isolate panels do not predict current Indian susceptibility or establish a clinical breakpoint; use isolate-specific interpretation.

indications.text: Inspected manufacturer insert lists urinary, respiratory, ENT and skin infections; Indian indication verification remains separate.

dosing.text: Bangladesh manufacturer adult UTI regimen, normal renal context: faropenem sodium 200–300 mg orally three times daily. Duration/maximum and Indian prescribing applicability require verification; not an ER or medoxomil regimen.

adjustments.text: The insert advises reduction or longer intervals in renal impairment but supplies no complete adjustment table.

pharmacokinetics.text: Oral faropenem pharmacokinetics vary between patients. A population analysis of 218 adults found creatinine clearance was an important determinant of apparent clearance, especially below 80 mL/min; food affected absorption rate and lag time. Reduced renal function can prolong elimination half-life. This study does not supply a validated Indian renal dose table.

pharmacodynamics.text: As a beta-lactam, faropenem activity is generally related to the fraction of the dosing interval that unbound concentrations exceed the MIC (fT>MIC). An HFS-TB model reported >62% T>MIC as a translational target against M. tuberculosis, but this is not a validated clinical target for routine bacterial infections, and susceptibility/breakpoint limitations prevent a universal bedside target.

safety.text: Diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, nausea and rash; severe beta-lactam hypersensitivity is a contraindication.

interactions.text: Insert discusses animal findings with cilastatin/furosemide and carbapenem–valproate reports; exact clinical faropenem interaction magnitude remains unresolved.

populations.text: This Bangladesh insert states pediatric safety below 18 years is unestablished; pregnancy/lactation require benefit–risk review.

administration.text: Immediate-release oral tablets may be taken with or without food in the inspected insert.

monitoring.text: No routine serum drug-monitoring target was identified. The population PK study found creatinine clearance affected faropenem clearance (especially below 80 mL/min) and food altered absorption; assess renal function when impairment is present, and monitor infection response, gastrointestinal intolerance and hypersensitivity. Use the local product label for any dose modification; no India-specific monitoring protocol was found.

stewardship.text: A verified Indian indication, local susceptibility and regimen review are required before any clinical use.

overview.text: Oral antistaphylococcal penicillin; systemic severe disease may require parenteral treatment.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, producing bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms.

spectrum.text: Selected Gram-positive organisms, including susceptible beta-lactamase-producing staphylococci.

pharmacodynamics.text: Class-level PK/PD summary: beta-lactam activity is linked to the proportion of the dosing interval that unbound drug remains above the organism MIC (%fT>MIC). A 2020 critically-ill-adult position paper summarizes preclinical efficacy targets of about 60–70% fT>MIC for penicillins and clinical ICU targets often spanning roughly 45–100%, depending on subclass and study. These are population-level evidence summaries, not an individual dose target. The appropriate exposure depends on the organism/MIC, infection site, severity, renal clearance, regimen and toxicity risk; prolonged infusion or therapeutic drug monitoring is a protocol-level decision. No validated drug-specific bedside target for this medicine and every Indian indication was verified.

safety.text: Avoid after flucloxacillin-associated jaundice/hepatic dysfunction; allergy and delayed hepatic injury are concerns.

interactions.text: Paracetamol coadministration can increase high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis risk, particularly in vulnerable patients.

populations.text: Pediatric oral doses are age-based in this data sheet; local neonatal schedules remain separate.

monitoring.text: Assess hepatic and renal function during prolonged therapy and investigate acidosis symptoms.

stewardship.text: Use culture results to confirm the need for antistaphylococcal therapy.

records.name: Gentamicin
forms: IV/IM gentamicin sulfate; topical, ophthalmic and otic products require separate route-specific profiles

overview.text: Parenteral aminoglycoside with concentration-dependent activity.

mechanism.text: Binds the prokaryotic ribosome and inhibits protein synthesis in susceptible bacteria.

spectrum.text: Selected aerobic Gram-negative bacilli; no activity against anaerobes. Resistance and clinical site limit use.

indications.text: NCDC includes gentamicin in selected Indian infection pathways; use should follow the syndrome recommendation and local susceptibility.

dosing.text:
Conventional adult dosing for serious infections with normal renal function is 1 mg/kg IV or IM every 8 hours, giving 3 mg/kg/day. Life-threatening infections may require up to 5 mg/kg/day in 3–4 divided doses, reduced as soon as clinically appropriate. Dose and interval require individualisation using renal function and serum concentrations. US prescribing information.

For eligible adults, an institutional extended-interval strategy uses 7 mg/kg IV every 24 hours when creatinine clearance is ≥60 mL/min, with timed concentrations and the specified nomogram determining subsequent intervals. This strategy is separate from conventional dosing. Endocarditis synergy, unstable renal function, pregnancy, neonatal treatment and other excluded populations require their own protocols. UCSF dosing guidance; SF VA aminoglycoside protocol.

adjustments.text: Renal elimination requires adjustment and close reassessment; dialysis and changing renal function need dedicated instructions.

pharmacokinetics.text: IM peaks generally occur within about an hour; IV infusion can produce similar concentrations; elimination is predominantly renal.

pharmacodynamics.text: Concentration-dependent killing; serum levels may be monitored to balance exposure and toxicity.

safety.text: Potentially irreversible auditory/vestibular toxicity, nephrotoxicity and neuromuscular blockade are major risks.

interactions.text: Other nephrotoxic/ototoxic agents and neuromuscular blockers may increase clinically important risk.

populations.text: Pregnancy, neonates, older adults and patients with renal, auditory or neuromuscular risk require special review.

administration.text: Administer separately; do not physically premix with other medicines. Follow compatible diluent and infusion instructions.

monitoring.text: Renal and eighth-cranial-nerve function; obtain drug levels according to the chosen protocol.

stewardship.text: Keep duration as short as effective, reassess cultures and discontinue redundant Gram-negative coverage.

Adult susceptible labeled infection, creatinine clearance ≥90 mL/min: imipenem 500 mg plus cilastatin 500 mg IV every 6 hours. Imipenem ceiling 4 g/day.

NTEP DR-TB regimen context (partial indication-specific addition): NTEP Table 3.7 lists imipenem 1 g plus cilastatin 1 g IV twice daily, with amoxicillin-clavulanate 125 mg as specified by that regimen. Use only in a specialist-designed longer oral M/XDR-TB regimen. This is not a standalone infection dose; other indication-specific dosing and adjustments still require separate review.

adjustments.text: Renal reductions begin below creatinine clearance 90 mL/min; use susceptibility-specific tables and dialysis restrictions.

pharmacokinetics.text: Both components have approximately one-hour plasma half-lives; kidney function affects clearance.

pharmacodynamics.text: Class-level PK/PD summary: beta-lactam activity is linked to the proportion of the dosing interval that unbound drug remains above the organism MIC (%fT>MIC). A 2020 critically-ill-adult position paper summarizes preclinical efficacy targets of about 60–70% fT>MIC for carbapenems / penems and clinical ICU targets often spanning roughly 45–100%, depending on subclass and study. These are population-level evidence summaries, not an individual dose target. The appropriate exposure depends on the organism/MIC, infection site, severity, renal clearance, regimen and toxicity risk; prolonged infusion or therapeutic drug monitoring is a protocol-level decision. No validated drug-specific bedside target for this medicine and every Indian indication was verified. For a fixed combination, this class summary does not establish the exposure target of the inhibitor component.

safety.text: Seizure risk increases with CNS disease or renal impairment; allergy and colitis occur.

interactions.text: Avoid valproate when possible; ganciclovir coadministration has been associated with seizures.

populations.text: Not indicated for meningitis; pediatric CNS infection and <30-kg renal impairment are important limitations.

administration.text: Infuse doses ≤500 mg over 20–30 minutes; larger doses require longer infusion.

monitoring.text: Follow renal function, neurologic status and organ-function tests with prolonged treatment.

stewardship.text: Use susceptibility results to reassess treatment; avoid use without a likely bacterial infection.

records.name: Isoniazid
forms: Oral tablets; exact Indian FDC ratios require separate records

overview.text: Core oral tuberculosis drug. This profile separates pharmacology from programme regimens; preventive treatment requires active disease to be excluded.

mechanism.text: Inhibits mycolic-acid production, disrupting the mycobacterial cell wall.

spectrum.text: Primarily susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis; resistance testing determines whether it remains an effective companion.

indications.text: Active TB in combination; selected TB preventive-treatment regimens after appropriate assessment.

dosing.text: India / NTEP context: adult DS-TB uses daily HRZE for 2 months then HRE for 4 months, with weight-band FDCs; the national workflow lists 5 mg/kg daily (usual range 4–6 mg/kg) for adults. In the NTEP 9–11-month shorter oral MDR/RR-TB regimen, high-dose isoniazid is 300 mg (16–29 kg), 600 mg (30–45 kg), or 900 mg (≥46 kg) daily. These are different regimen contexts and must not be interchanged.

adjustments.text: An Indian Society of Critical Care Medicine position statement reports that isoniazid and rifampicin do not require dose adjustment in renal failure. This is a general renal statement; severe hepatic disease, interactions, dialysis timing, weight-band formulation and the full NTEP regimen still require specialist review.

pharmacokinetics.text: Oral absorption falls with food; acetylation rate varies substantially between patients.

pharmacodynamics.text: A systematic review/meta-analysis found low 2-hour post-dose concentrations in a pooled 43% of studied patients for isoniazid; only 3 of 12 studies examining outcomes found an association between low concentration and unsuccessful treatment. The authors noted uncertainty around accepted concentration thresholds. This supports selective specialist TDM in suspected malabsorption, delayed response or unusual risk, but does not establish a universal target or authorize automatic dose escalation. Use the complete NTEP combination regimen and susceptibility results.

safety.text: Potentially fatal hepatitis and peripheral neuropathy are major hazards; risk increases with alcohol and selected patient factors.

interactions.text: Can increase phenytoin exposure; aluminium antacids reduce absorption. Review alcohol and tyramine-rich foods.

populations.text: Pregnancy, malnutrition, diabetes and neuropathy risk require assessment of pyridoxine supplementation.

administration.text: Give oral tablets according to the selected programme regimen; label advises administration without food.

monitoring.text: Assess hepatitis symptoms and neurological complaints regularly; obtain liver tests when baseline risk or symptoms warrant.

stewardship.text: Do not use as monotherapy for active TB; confirm susceptibility and support uninterrupted combination treatment.

records.name: Levofloxacin
forms: Oral tablet/solution and IV infusion; exact Indian products require verification

overview.text: Systemic antibacterial medicine; exact salts, route and formulation must be confirmed against the Indian product. [TB regimen note below is indication-specific.]

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication and repair.

spectrum.text: Susceptibility is organism- and resistance-specific. For TB, use molecular/phenotypic drug-susceptibility results and NTEP regimen criteria; do not infer activity from class alone.

indications.text: Used in selected NTEP drug-resistant TB regimens and isoniazid-resistant TB regimens; routine bacterial indications are product-label dependent and require current Indian guideline review.

dosing.text: India / NTEP adult DR-TB context: daily dose in the 9–11-month shorter oral, longer oral M/XDR-TB and H-mono/poly-resistant TB tables is 250 mg (16–29 kg), 750 mg (30–45 kg), or 1,000 mg (≥46 kg). This is not a general infection dose; regimen choice requires susceptibility, eligibility and expert review.

adjustments.text: The product label requires renal dose adjustment below its stated creatinine-clearance threshold; use the exact local product table and renal function, especially with dialysis.

pharmacokinetics.text: High oral bioavailability (about 99% for common tablet strengths); peak usually within 1–2 hours; largely renally excreted unchanged.

pharmacodynamics.text: Concentration/exposure relative to organism MIC is relevant to antibacterial activity; no individual TB dose calculator or validated bedside exposure target is supplied here.

safety.text: Serious class warnings include tendinitis/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects and worsening myasthenia gravis; QT, dysglycemia and aortic risks require review.

interactions.text: Oral iron, zinc, magnesium, aluminum and other polyvalent cations reduce absorption; separate doses. Review QT-prolonging drugs, warfarin and seizure risk.

populations.text: Use in children and pregnancy only when a specific risk-benefit indication supports it; renal function and older age affect safety.

administration.text: Oral with or without food; IV infusion only at label rate. Keep mineral products separated as directed by the exact product label.

monitoring.text: Review renal function, tendon/neurologic symptoms, glucose and ECG when risk factors or regimen require.

stewardship.text: For TB, use only in a complete susceptibility-guided regimen under NTEP/specialist oversight; never use as monotherapy. For other infections, follow current Indian syndrome guidance, cultures and susceptibility results.

records.name: Linezolid
forms: Oral tablets/suspension; IV infusion

overview.text: Oxazolidinone active against selected Gram-positive bacteria; oral bioavailability supports route switch in suitable cases.

mechanism.text: Binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and prevents formation of the initiation complex.

spectrum.text: Includes susceptible MRSA and VRE; no Gram-negative activity.

indications.text: NCDC includes linezolid in selected resistant Gram-positive pathways; verify organism, syndrome and local guidance.

dosing.text:
For labelled pneumonia, complicated skin and skin-structure infection, and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium infection, adults and adolescents aged ≥12 years generally receive 600 mg IV or PO every 12 hours. Labelled durations are 10–14 days for pneumonia and complicated skin infection and 14–28 days for VRE infection. Children from birth through 11 years generally receive 10 mg/kg every 8 hours; most preterm neonates younger than 7 days require a special initial every-12-hour schedule. No dose change is required solely when switching between IV and oral administration. US prescribing information.

Drug-resistant TB requires regimen-specific dosing, including 600 mg once daily in specified WHO regimens, rather than the every-12-hour schedule used for the bacterial indications above. WHO TB operational handbook, 2025.

adjustments.text: Parent-drug dose adjustment is generally not specified for renal impairment in the cited label, but metabolites accumulate; dialysis timing and toxicity risk need review.

pharmacokinetics.text: Near-complete oral bioavailability; nonenzymatic oxidation; parent drug elimination is partly nonrenal.

pharmacodynamics.text: Time-dependent antibacterial effect is described; monitoring and duration are important due to cumulative toxicity.

safety.text: Myelosuppression, neuropathy, lactic acidosis, serotonin syndrome and visual toxicity are important risks, especially with prolonged treatment.

interactions.text: MAO inhibition creates interactions with serotonergic and adrenergic agents; review antidepressants, opioids and sympathomimetics.

populations.text: Pregnancy and pediatric use require age-specific evidence; review baseline cytopenia and interacting therapies.

administration.text: Oral and IV forms have high oral bioavailability, but transition must follow clinical and product guidance.

monitoring.text: CBC at baseline and at least weekly during therapy as directed by labeling; assess vision/neuropathy and serotonin toxicity when relevant.

stewardship.text: Use targeted therapy for resistant Gram-positive infection; avoid unnecessary overlap with other anti-MRSA agents.

records.name: Meropenem
forms: Meropenem trihydrate powder, 500 mg or 1 g, for IV use.

overview.text: Broad-spectrum IV carbapenem; no cilastatin is required.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, producing bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms.

spectrum.text: Selected susceptible Gram-negative, Gram-positive and anaerobic organisms; carbapenem resistance remains clinically important.

indications.text: Indian label additionally covers pneumonia, UTI, gynecological infection, meningitis, septicemia and adult febrile neutropenia; US indication scope differs.

dosing.text:
Indian-label adult bacterial meningitis, creatinine clearance >50 mL/min: 2 g IV every 8 hours, usually over 15–30 minutes. Other infection examples use 500 mg–1 g every 8 hours.

NTEP DR-TB regimen context (partial indication-specific addition): NTEP longer oral M/XDR-TB table: 1,000 mg IV three times daily, with 2,000 mg twice daily listed as an alternative; use with amoxicillin-clavulanate 125 mg as specified. This is a specialist-designed combination regimen, not ordinary meropenem monotherapy dosing. This is not a standalone infection dose; other indication-specific dosing and adjustments still require separate review.

adjustments.text: At creatinine clearance ≤50 mL/min use the renal table; pediatric renal and CRRT schedules are not established here.

pharmacokinetics.text: Low protein binding, approximately 2%; predominantly renal elimination.

pharmacodynamics.text: Time with free concentrations above MIC relates to antibacterial effect; a patient-specific target is not prescribed here.

safety.text: Anaphylaxis, seizures, colitis, thrombocytopenia and rhabdomyolysis are recognized risks.

interactions.text: Valproate concentrations can fall markedly; avoid this combination where possible. Probenecid increases exposure.

populations.text: Neonatal intra-abdominal regimens depend on gestational/postnatal age; use the separate table.

administration.text: Check diluent-specific stability; do not mix with other medicines without verified compatibility.

monitoring.text: Assess renal function, neurologic symptoms, counts and muscle symptoms as indicated.

stewardship.text: Use susceptibility results to reassess treatment; avoid use without a likely bacterial infection.

records.name: Metronidazole
forms: Oral tablets/suspension; IV infusion; topical and vaginal products require separate profiles

overview.text: Nitroimidazole with antibacterial and antiprotozoal uses; formulations are route-specific.

mechanism.text: Reduced in susceptible anaerobes/protozoa to reactive intermediates that damage nucleic acids.

spectrum.text: Active against many obligate anaerobes and selected protozoa; not aerobic bacteria.

indications.text: NCDC includes metronidazole in selected Indian intra-abdominal, anaerobic and protozoal pathways; site and diagnosis determine the regimen.

dosing.text:
For serious anaerobic bacterial infection, the adult oral label recommends 7.5 mg/kg every 6 hours, maximum 4 g/day. Serious infection may initially require IV therapy. The labelled usual duration is 7–10 days, with longer courses for selected deep infections. US prescribing information.

For bacterial vaginosis, administer 500 mg PO twice daily for 7 days. For trichomoniasis, CDC recommends 500 mg PO twice daily for 7 days in women and 2 g PO once in men. CDC treatment summary; CDC trichomoniasis guideline.

For acute intestinal amoebiasis, labelled dosing is 750 mg PO three times daily for 5–10 days in adults and 35–50 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for 10 days in children. These doses form part of an indication-specific treatment pathway. US prescribing information: amoebiasis.

adjustments.text: Severe hepatic impairment requires dose reduction consideration; assess dialysis timing and exact product labeling.

pharmacokinetics.text: Orally well absorbed; hepatic metabolism; metabolites and parent compound are excreted in urine.

pharmacodynamics.text: Clinical PK/PD targets are not presented as a routine bedside metric in the inspected tablet source.

safety.text: Peripheral neuropathy, encephalopathy/seizures, blood dyscrasias, hypersensitivity and C. difficile-associated diarrhea can occur.

interactions.text: Review warfarin/INR, lithium, disulfiram and alcohol-containing products; consult the complete label for interactions.

populations.text: Pregnancy trimester, lactation, hepatic disease and prolonged courses need indication-specific review.

administration.text: Use formulation-specific directions; oral and IV schedules should be reconciled rather than presumed equivalent.

monitoring.text: Clinical response, neurological symptoms during prolonged use, CBC when indicated and INR with warfarin.

stewardship.text: Do not add anaerobic coverage when the selected regimen already provides it; review duration and source control.

forms: Oral tablet and IV infusion; exact Indian products require verification

overview.text: Systemic antibacterial medicine; exact salts, route and formulation must be confirmed against the Indian product. [TB regimen note below is indication-specific.]

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.

spectrum.text: Susceptibility is organism- and resistance-specific. For TB, use molecular/phenotypic drug-susceptibility results and NTEP regimen criteria; do not infer activity from class alone.

indications.text: Used in NTEP BPaLM, shorter oral and longer oral drug-resistant TB regimens; routine bacterial indications are product-label dependent and require current Indian guideline review.

dosing.text: India / NTEP context: BPaLM uses 400 mg orally once daily for weeks 1–26, with extension criteria potentially through week 39. Longer oral M/XDR-TB adult table lists 200 mg (16–29 kg) and 400 mg (≥30 kg); high-dose moxifloxacin is a separate specialist-selected option. Do not transfer these doses to routine bacterial infection treatment.

adjustments.text: No renal dose adjustment is generally required by the inspected product label; confirm hepatic restrictions and local product information.

pharmacokinetics.text: Oral bioavailability is high (approximately 90%); distributes widely; elimination includes hepatic metabolism and renal/fecal routes.

pharmacodynamics.text: Concentration/exposure relative to organism MIC is relevant to antibacterial activity; no individual TB dose calculator or validated bedside exposure target is supplied here.

safety.text: QT prolongation is a key risk; also tendon injury, neuropathy, CNS effects, dysglycemia and exacerbation of myasthenia gravis.

interactions.text: Separate oral doses from antacids/iron/zinc/magnesium; avoid or closely review other QT-prolonging drugs. NTEP BPaLM requires careful interaction review.

populations.text: Avoid in known QT prolongation and use caution with hepatic disease, electrolyte abnormalities, older adults and pregnancy; follow regimen-specific pediatric guidance.

administration.text: Oral or IV infusion; do not administer as IV push. Switching route follows product-specific instructions.

monitoring.text: ECG/QTc, potassium/magnesium, hepatic tests and adverse-effect review per NTEP regimen; monitor other QT-active companions.

stewardship.text: For TB, use only in a complete susceptibility-guided regimen under NTEP/specialist oversight; never use as monotherapy. For other infections, follow current Indian syndrome guidance, cultures and susceptibility results.

records.name: Nafithromycin
forms: Oral 400 mg tablets

overview.text: India-developed respiratory antibacterial, marketed as MIQNAF.

mechanism.text: Innovator description hosted on the Government of India BIRAC portal reports binding at two sites on 23S rRNA in the bacterial ribosome, inhibiting protein synthesis. This is an innovator-reported mechanism summary, not a substitute for the approved Indian prescribing information.

spectrum.text: Manufacturer describes respiratory-pathogen activity; local susceptibility still matters.

indications.text: Adult community-acquired bacterial pneumonia under the cited Indian authorization.

dosing.text: Government of India confirms authorization of 400 mg tablets for adults (≥18 years) with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia. The published Indian phase III regimen was 800 mg orally once daily for 3 days (two 400 mg tablets per dose), studied in adults with PORT risk class II–IV. Apply only within the current approved Indian indication and product insert; do not generalize to children, other infections, severe/complicated disease or combination regimens.

adjustments.text:
Renal impairment: the Indian PI provides no reduced-dose schedule for mild or moderate impairment; these groups received the standard regimen in clinical trials. Nafithromycin is not recommended when creatinine clearance is <30 mL/min. Dedicated renal-impairment PK has not been established. Section 4.4 also advises against use when renal and hepatic impairment coexist; section 4.6 specifically repeats the restriction for severe renal impairment with hepatic impairment. Indian PI, §§4.2, 4.4 and 4.6.

The phase III trial did include renal impairment: 21/241 nafithromycin recipients in the modified intention-to-treat population had CrCl 30–60 mL/min, and 58/241 had CrCl >60–90 mL/min; none had CrCl <30 mL/min. Therefore, the earlier statement that all renal impairment was excluded is incorrect. Pophale et al., Table 1.

Hepatic impairment: the PI states that dose adjustment would not be required across mild, moderate or severe impairment, but bases this on extrapolation from other macrolides and anticipated compensatory renal elimination. Nafithromycin-specific impairment data are unavailable, and treatment requires an individual benefit–risk assessment. The PI separately lists a history of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction, including with or without prior macrolide exposure, as a contraindication; conditional dose advice does not override that contraindication. Indian PI, §§4.3–4.4 and 4.6.

Unresolved evidence gaps: dedicated impairment PK, dialysis removal/dosing, and clinical validation of the hepatic extrapolation. The relationship between the broad hepatic-history contraindication and conditional hepatic-impairment advice requires manufacturer/regulatory clarification before conversion into an automated prescribing rule.

The linked 2026 review does not report dedicated nafithromycin pharmacokinetic studies in hepatic or renal impairment, dialysis removal, or validated dose changes. Its general statement about hepatic and renal elimination does not establish compensatory clearance or an adjustment rule; follow the Indian PI restrictions and retain the uncertainties above. IJPS review, 2026.

source_inclusion_approval.scope: Approval covers inclusion and citation of the listed references in the antibiotic module; it is not clinical validation or approval for treatment decisions.

pharmacokinetics.text:
In healthy-adult phase I studies, single oral doses of 100–1,200 mg produced mean Cmax values of 0.099–1.742 mg/L and AUC0–t values of 0.54–22.53 h·mg/L. With repeated once-daily dosing for 7 days (600, 800 or 1,000 mg), day-7 Cmax was 1.340–2.987 mg/L and AUC0–24 was 13.48–43.46 h·mg/L; steady state was reached around day 3 for 600/800 mg and day 4 for 1,000 mg. Exposure increased more than dose proportionally and showed moderate accumulation. Food increased AUC by about 1.2-fold at the studied 400/800 mg single doses. These are phase I healthy-volunteer values, not dosing guidance for organ impairment. Phase I study.

After 800 mg once daily for 3 days in healthy adults, concentrations in epithelial lining fluid (ELF) were 2.5–36.3 times plasma concentrations over 48 hours; mean ELF/plasma AUC24 ratio was 13.8 and alveolar-macrophage/plasma AUC24 ratio was 527. These ratios compare total plasma concentrations and are site-specific PK observations, not proof of efficacy for every respiratory pathogen or patient. Rodvold et al.

The available phase I paper reported about 80% plasma-protein binding and recovery of unchanged nafithromycin in urine and feces after single dosing. Dedicated PK studies in significant renal or hepatic impairment and dialysis have not established a dose algorithm; use the Indian product information for the approved adult CABP regimen and restrictions. Phase I study; Indian PI.

pharmacodynamics.text:
Nafithromycin is a ketolide that binds the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit at regions of 23S rRNA and inhibits protein synthesis. The Indian product information describes activity against selected pneumococci with erm(B) and/or mef(A) resistance mechanisms; this does not mean every macrolide-resistant isolate is susceptible. Indian MIQNAF PI, §§5.1–5.2; IJPS review, 2026.

AUC/MIC is the leading candidate exposure-response index based on macrolide/ketolide pharmacology and nafithromycin preclinical models. The human lung-PK study measured high ELF and alveolar-macrophage exposure, but did not validate a patient-level efficacy threshold. Experimental model estimates reported in the literature (including ELF AUC24/MIC estimates) are not validated plasma targets or routine TDM targets and must not be used to alter individual doses. Rodvold et al.; IJPS review, 2026.

In the Indian phase III adult CABP trial, the studied 800 mg once-daily, 3-day regimen was non-inferior to 7-day moxifloxacin on early clinical response. This trial outcome supports the approved regimen for its studied indication; it does not establish a universal AUC/MIC target. Pophale et al., 2025; Indian PI.

Unresolved evidence gap: no prospectively validated human efficacy exposure threshold or therapeutic-drug-monitoring target is established. The IJPS review is secondary context and does not change this limitation.

source_inclusion_approval.scope: Approval covers inclusion and citation of the listed references in the antibiotic module; it is not clinical validation or approval for treatment decisions.

safety.text: In the Indian phase III trial (244 nafithromycin-treated adults), treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 20.1%; common events ≥2% included abdominal pain (3.7%), nausea (2.9%), headache (6.1%) and diarrhoea (2.0%), mostly mild; no serious adverse events or deaths were reported in that group. Follow-up and sample size cannot exclude rare or delayed harms. The trial reported no clinically meaningful ECG/liver lab group differences, but this is not proof of zero QT or hepatic risk; use the approved Indian product information and pharmacovigilance updates.

interactions.text:
The Indian PI states that no human clinical drug-interaction studies have been conducted. Human-liver-microsome experiments demonstrate weak CYP3A inhibition, but this does not establish an absence of clinically relevant interactions. The PI also identifies nafithromycin as a P-glycoprotein substrate and inhibitor and an OATP1B1/OATP1B3 inhibitor. Indian PI, §4.5; Chavan et al., 2021.

Apply the following PI recommendations:

- Moderate/strong CYP3A and P-gp inducers: concomitant use is not recommended because nafithromycin exposure and efficacy may decrease. Examples include rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital and St John’s wort.
- CYP3A inhibitors or P-gp inhibitors: prescribe cautiously because nafithromycin exposure may increase.
- Sensitive P-gp substrates with a narrow therapeutic window: use cautiously because substrate exposure may increase; examples include digoxin, colchicine and tacrolimus.
- Sensitive OATP1B1/OATP1B3 substrates: use cautiously; the PI lists examples including statins and repaglinide.
- Medicines with a narrow therapeutic window that prolong QT: do not use concurrently. Indian PI, §§4.4–4.5.

The available PMC phase 1 clinical paper studied single/multiple doses and food effects in healthy volunteers; it did not test coadministration with interacting medicines. The Indian PI interaction precautions remain based on nonclinical/in-vitro findings rather than human pair-specific DDI estimates. PMC phase 1 study and Indian PI.

Unresolved evidence gap: interaction magnitude and validated pair-specific dose changes in humans remain unknown. The PI’s quantitative findings—including midazolam and digoxin experiments—come from animal or in-vitro studies. Its avoidance/caution recommendations should not be represented as results of human coadministration trials. Indian PI, §4.5.

The linked review describes generally favorable interaction properties, but does not provide human coadministration DDI estimates. It therefore does not change the PI-based precautions or resolve the interaction-magnitude gap above. IJPS review, 2026.

populations.text: Adult authorization; do not extrapolate to children or pregnancy.

administration.text: Oral tablets; verify current food and administration instructions from PI.

monitoring.text:
Before treatment, review macrolide allergy, hepatic history, renal function, concomitant medicines, QT-risk history and myasthenia gravis. Avoid use in congenital/acquired QT prolongation, cardiac arrhythmia or severe cardiac insufficiency. If treatment cannot be avoided in a patient predisposed to QT prolongation, perform ECG monitoring during treatment. Indian PI, §§4.3–4.4.

Assess hepatic symptoms—including jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, anorexia and right-upper-abdominal pain—with liver tests and other relevant investigations. Discontinue immediately if hepatic dysfunction develops. Evaluate significant diarrhoea for C. difficile, and discontinue treatment with urgent assessment for worsening myasthenia gravis or serious hypersensitivity. Indian PI, §§4.4 and 9.

Do not automatically extend or repeat the three-day course. The PI reports more transaminase elevations with five-day than three-day treatment in phase II and advises considering another antibiotic for frequent recurrent CABP. The phase III trial reported no Hy’s-law cases and no nafithromycin recipients meeting its combined QTcF >500 ms and >60 ms increase criterion; rare toxicity remains possible. Indian PI, §4.4; primary phase III safety results.

Phase 1 safety context: small healthy-volunteer studies included ECG, vital-sign and laboratory surveillance; three participants had transient asymptomatic ALT/AST elevations below 2× ULN, with no clinically significant ECG or laboratory trend reported. These short, small studies cannot exclude uncommon or delayed toxicity and do not define an outpatient monitoring schedule. Phase 1 nafithromycin study.

Unresolved evidence gap: the PI does not specify a universal laboratory-testing schedule or ECG timetable for every low-risk three-day course. Additional investigations should follow individual risk and clinical findings. No routine therapeutic-drug-monitoring target is established.

The linked review summarizes tolerability favorably but does not establish an outpatient ECG/laboratory monitoring schedule or a validated TDM target. The PI’s risk-based instructions and the limits of the phase I/III safety datasets remain applicable. IJPS review, 2026.

records.name: Ofloxacin
forms: Oral tablets; ophthalmic and otic drops are separate products and require distinct profiles

overview.text: Fluoroquinolone available in systemic and route-specific topical formulations.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.

spectrum.text: Selected susceptible Gram-negative and other organisms; resistance and site-specific breakpoints limit coverage.

indications.text: NCDC includes ofloxacin in selected Indian urinary/epididymal pathways; use current syndrome guidance and susceptibility.

dosing.text:
Adult oral dosing is 200–400 mg every 12 hours, selected according to the infection and renal function. Labelled examples include 200 mg every 12 hours for 10 days for complicated UTI, 300 mg every 12 hours for 6 weeks for E. coli prostatitis, and 400 mg every 12 hours for 10 days for pneumonia. After a normal initial dose, creatinine clearance 20–50 mL/min requires the usual unit dose every 24 hours; <20 mL/min requires half the usual unit dose every 24 hours. US prescribing information.

These labelled schedules do not establish preferred empirical treatment. Ofloxacin is no longer recommended as a component of WHO longer MDR-TB regimens. WHO TB operational handbook, 2025.

adjustments.text: Systemic dose adjustment is needed in renal impairment using the product-specific table.

pharmacokinetics.text: Oral bioavailability is about 98%; renal excretion predominates; concentrations peak within approximately 1–2 hours.

pharmacodynamics.text: Fluoroquinolone activity relates to AUC/MIC and peak/MIC measures; a universal patient-specific target is not encoded.

safety.text: Tendon injury, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, exacerbation of myasthenia gravis, QT effects and dysglycemia are important risks.

interactions.text: Separate oral doses from mineral-containing antacids/supplements; review QT-prolonging agents and anticoagulants.

populations.text: Pregnancy and children require specific risk-benefit assessment; avoid casual extrapolation from topical drops.

administration.text: Do not interchange oral, IV, ophthalmic and otic doses; follow preparation and timing instructions for the exact product.

monitoring.text: Renal function, tendon/neurologic symptoms and ECG/glucose monitoring where patient risks warrant.

stewardship.text: Avoid empirical use where resistance is high; culture, de-escalate and reserve systemic fluoroquinolones for a valid indication.

forms: Potassium salt oral tablets, 250 mg or 500 mg.

overview.text: Acid-stable oral penicillin intended for selected mild-to-moderate infections.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, producing bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms.

spectrum.text: Susceptible streptococci and pneumococci; penicillinase-producing bacteria are not covered.

pharmacodynamics.text: Class-level PK/PD summary: beta-lactam activity is linked to the proportion of the dosing interval that unbound drug remains above the organism MIC (%fT>MIC). A 2020 critically-ill-adult position paper summarizes preclinical efficacy targets of about 60–70% fT>MIC for penicillins and clinical ICU targets often spanning roughly 45–100%, depending on subclass and study. These are population-level evidence summaries, not an individual dose target. The appropriate exposure depends on the organism/MIC, infection site, severity, renal clearance, regimen and toxicity risk; prolonged infusion or therapeutic drug monitoring is a protocol-level decision. interactions.text: Bacteriostatic antibiotics can antagonize penicillin activity; review the label interaction cautions.

populations.text: Excretion is delayed in neonates and young infants; no neonatal dose is inferred.

administration.text: May be taken with meals; exposure is somewhat higher when fasting.

monitoring.text: Assess clinical response and hypersensitivity; persistent diarrhea requires evaluation.

stewardship.text: The label contains historical prophylaxis advice; current national guidance must determine modern prophylactic use.

records.name: Polymyxin B
forms: Parenteral polymyxin B sulfate; local combinations require separate product profiles

overview.text: Active polymyxin; distinct from colistimethate sodium.

mechanism.text: Binds bacterial membranes and disrupts permeability.

spectrum.text: Susceptible aerobic Gram-negative organisms; intrinsic resistance limits coverage.

indications.text: Selected serious resistant Gram-negative infections.

dosing.text:
For severe infection in adults, the international consensus recommends an IV loading dose of 2–2.5 mg/kg using total body weight over 1 hour, followed by 1.25–1.5 mg/kg every 12 hours over 1 hour. 1 mg polymyxin B equals 10,000 IU. Unlike colistimethate sodium, the consensus does not recommend automatic maintenance-dose reduction for renal impairment or dose adjustment solely because of renal replacement therapy. This differs from older product-label advice; renal function and toxicity still require close monitoring. International polymyxin consensus, recommendations R15–R18.

These are specialist dosing recommendations for situations in which polymyxin B has been selected; they do not establish it as preferred treatment when safer effective alternatives are available. IDSA AMR guidance.

adjustments.text: JIPMER 2026 and WHO AWaRe indicate no routine renal dose adjustment for polymyxin B, unlike colistimethate. JIPMER recommends adjusted body weight for obesity; WHO adult schedule is not a complete pediatric or renal replacement therapy protocol. Confirm indication and institution-specific guidance.

pharmacokinetics.text: Parenteral administration; poor tissue distribution and renal toxicity are key limitations.

pharmacodynamics.text:
Polymyxin B is administered as an active antibacterial. It binds bacterial LPS/lipid A and disrupts membranes. Recent mechanistic work indicates that bacterial metabolic activity contributes to the outer-membrane changes preceding lethal inner-membrane injury. Primary mechanistic study.

In a murine Klebsiella pneumoniae study, unbound AUC/MIC correlated with efficacy in thigh infection. Targets for a 1-log bacterial reduction ranged from 3.72 to 28.0; bacteriostasis was not achieved in lung infection at the highest tolerated dose. These values are animal-model findings. Primary polymyxin B PK/PD study.

Unresolved evidence gap: These experimental targets are not universally validated human thresholds. Polymyxin B and colistimethate sodium differ in administration, clearance and urinary exposure; their PK/PD and dosing assumptions are not interchangeable.

A 2025 systematic review of adult PK studies likewise found substantial variability and renal-function covariates, but it does not establish an efficacy exposure threshold. The international consensus notes that evidence is insufficient to define a polymyxin B AUC target for efficacy. It describes Css,avg 2–4 mg/L (AUCss,24 about 50–100 mg·h/L) only as a possible toxicity-acceptable range, not as a validated efficacy target; higher exposures risk nephrotoxicity. The recommendation is partly extrapolated from colistin and preclinical work, and the guideline calls for more clinical efficacy and safety data. International polymyxin consensus. It describes total average steady-state concentrations of 2–4 mg/L (AUCss,24 about 50–100 mg·h/L) only as a possible toxicity-acceptable range, not as a validated efficacy target; higher exposures risk nephrotoxicity. International polymyxin consensus.

records.name: Pretomanid
forms: Oral 200 mg tablets

overview.text: Component of specific short all-oral resistant-TB regimens. US label scope and Indian BPaLM guidance must be kept distinct.

mechanism.text: Activated by mycobacterial enzymes; disrupts mycolic-acid synthesis and respiratory processes under different growth conditions.

spectrum.text: Susceptible M. tuberculosis; resistance to regimen components undermines effectiveness.

indications.text: Indian guidance includes eligible patients in BPaLM; the US label is a narrower BPaL indication.

dosing.text: India / NTEP BPaLM context only: 200 mg orally once daily with food for weeks 1–26; NTEP extension criteria may extend treatment through week 39. It is used only with bedaquiline, linezolid and moxifloxacin in eligible programmatic patients, with regimen-specific monitoring. Do not use as monotherapy or extrapolate this dose to another combination.

adjustments.text:
The US label continues to describe the effects of renal/hepatic impairment as unknown. However, primary human impairment results now exist, so an unqualified statement that no human data are available should be removed. US pretomanid label, §§8.6–8.7.

Renal evidence: NCT03896750 evaluated a single 200 mg dose in five participants with severe renal impairment, one with end-stage renal disease not receiving dialysis, and six matched controls. Parent-drug exposure was not increased in the impaired groups in this small study; metabolite exposures differed. Results were first posted on 15 October 2025. Primary registry results.

Hepatic evidence: NCT02422524 enrolled six participants with mild impairment, two with moderate impairment and six controls; none with severe impairment. Mean AUC0–∞ after a single 200 mg dose was 34.8, 55.9 and 30.7 µg·h/mL, respectively. The study terminated before completing its planned cohorts. Results were first posted on 5 March 2025. Primary registry results.

A population-PK analysis found that baseline renal/hepatic biomarkers were evaluated as covariates and reported small modeled effects in its studied populations; the authors noted dedicated renal/hepatic impairment studies were ongoing. Mass-balance data cited in that paper found <1% of parent drug excreted unchanged in urine, but the authors caution renal disease may affect absorption, metabolism or distribution. This does not establish a no-adjustment rule. PMC population-PK study.

A clinical pharmacology review summarizes liver-enzyme abnormalities across pretomanid trials and reports higher hepatic-event frequencies in multidrug regimens than with pretomanid monotherapy; attribution to pretomanid versus companion drugs is uncertain. This supports regimen-level hepatic vigilance, not an organ-function dose formula. PMC review.

Unresolved evidence gap: these small single-dose studies do not establish an approved numerical adjustment algorithm, severe-hepatic or dialysis dosing, or safety across a full BPaL/BPaLM course. An Indian product-specific adjustment instruction was not verified in this update.

Organ-impairment evidence remains limited: a rifamycin interaction trial excluded participants with ALT >3× ULN, bilirubin >2× ULN or creatinine above ULN, so it cannot establish dosing in significant hepatic or renal impairment. In that study, rifampin reduced pretomanid exposure versus rifabutin; this is an interaction finding and should follow current product/regimen restrictions, not be converted into a pretomanid dose increase. PMC-PRETOMANID-RIFAMYCIN-TRIAL-2021.

forms: Oral 250 mg film-coated tablets; WHO source uses spelling protionamide

overview.text: Reserve thioamide related to ethionamide. The WHO-hosted SRA text establishes pharmacology, not current Indian marketing or programme preference.

mechanism.text: The SmPC infers inhibition of InhA-mediated mycolic-acid synthesis from structural similarity to ethionamide.

spectrum.text: M. tuberculosis and selected nontuberculous mycobacteria when susceptibility is demonstrated.

indications.text: Second-line combination therapy where first-line treatment is unsuitable; species-specific susceptibility is necessary.

dosing.text:
Adult dosing is 15–20 mg/kg/day PO, maximum 1 g/day, usually administered once daily. Two divided doses or gradual dose escalation may improve gastrointestinal tolerability. Prothionamide must be used as part of an appropriate multidrug TB regimen. WHO TB operational handbook, Annex 1, 2025.

MSF’s 2025 operational guidance also specifies 15–20 mg/kg once daily for children, maximum 1 g/day, using its weight-band dosing table. Regimen eligibility and paediatric dosing should follow the applicable national TB programme. MSF Tuberculosis, Appendix 10.

adjustments.text: Severe hepatic disease and severe renal dysfunction need special review; the SmPC contains renal guidance that is not transcribed here.

pharmacokinetics.text: Orally absorbed and hepatically metabolized; little drug is removed by hemodialysis. Pediatric PK data are sparse.

pharmacodynamics.text: Activity can be static or cidal depending on conditions; ethionamide and prothionamide show complete cross-resistance in the SmPC.

safety.text: Marked gastrointestinal intolerance, hepatic injury, neurological symptoms and thyroid disturbance require surveillance.

interactions.text: Alcohol increases CNS effects; review hepatotoxic companions and anticoagulation-related risks in the full interaction section.

populations.text: The source restricts pregnancy/lactation use; do not infer safety from an ethionamide regimen.

administration.text: Oral tablets require the formulation-specific instructions; gradual introduction may be used under specialist supervision to improve tolerance.

monitoring.text: Monitor liver function and neurological/psychiatric symptoms; assess glucose and thyroid effects during prolonged treatment.

stewardship.text: Do not count ethionamide and prothionamide as two independent effective drugs in a regimen.

dosing.text: India / NTEP context: adult DS-TB uses daily HRZE for 2 months followed by HRE for 4 months; the national workflow lists pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg daily (usual range 20–30 mg/kg) for adults. Adult DR-TB tables instead list 750 mg (16–29 kg), 1,250 mg (30–45 kg), 1,750 mg (46–70 kg), or 2,000 mg (>70 kg) daily. Use the selected NTEP regimen and assess hepatic risk; do not apply one schedule across regimens.

adjustments.text: For stage IV–V CKD or haemodialysis, an ISCCM India position statement cites pyrazinamide 25–30 mg/kg three times weekly because elimination/metabolite clearance may be delayed. This is specialist renal-failure guidance, not the routine daily NTEP schedule; coordinate dose timing with dialysis and the complete regimen.

pharmacokinetics.text: Hepatic conversion yields pyrazinoic acid; metabolites are renally eliminated. Half-life is prolonged with renal or hepatic dysfunction.

pharmacodynamics.text: A systematic review/meta-analysis found low 2-hour post-dose concentrations in a pooled 12% of studied patients for pyrazinamide; only 3 of 12 studies examining outcomes found an association between low concentration and unsuccessful treatment. The authors noted uncertainty around accepted concentration thresholds. This supports selective specialist TDM in suspected malabsorption, delayed response or unusual risk, but does not establish a universal target or authorize automatic dose escalation. Use the complete NTEP combination regimen and susceptibility results.

safety.text: Hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia are prominent; acute gout or severe hepatic damage are contraindications.

interactions.text: May interfere with urine ketone assays; review combined hepatotoxic therapy and alcohol exposure.

populations.text: Pregnancy and lactation require programme risk assessment; small amounts enter milk. Older patients need cautious organ-function review.

administration.text: Administer orally with effective companion TB drugs; avoid inferring tablet counts from the tablet strength alone.

monitoring.text: Baseline liver tests and uric acid; reassess jaundice, anorexia, persistent vomiting or painful swollen joints.

stewardship.text: Use the full susceptibility-guided regimen; neither isolated hyperuricemia nor a positive culture should trigger unsupervised regimen changes.

records.name: Rifabutin
forms: Oral 150 mg capsules in inspected US label

overview.text: Oral rifamycin with a different interaction profile from rifampicin. Substitution requires individual antiretroviral and TB-regimen review.

mechanism.text: Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase in susceptible organisms.

spectrum.text: Active against M. avium complex; in-vitro M. tuberculosis activity does not replace susceptibility and regimen assessment.

indications.text: US label indicates prevention of disseminated MAC in advanced HIV; TB substitution is not a directly transferable label indication.

dosing.text:
For active drug-susceptible TB, rifabutin is administered within a combination regimen, generally at 5 mg/kg PO once daily, usual dose 300 mg, when the accompanying medicines permit that dose. Antiretroviral interactions can require substantial dose modification; the exact ART regimen must be checked before prescribing. NIH HIV/TB dosing guidance.

For prevention of disseminated MAC, the US label recommends 300 mg PO once daily; 150 mg twice daily with food may improve gastrointestinal tolerability. US prescribing information.

NIH lists 300 mg daily as an alternative MAC-prophylaxis regimen when preferred macrolides cannot be used. Exclude active TB before prophylaxis; primary MAC prophylaxis is generally unnecessary when effective ART is initiated promptly. Active mycobacterial disease requires combination treatment. NIH MAC guideline.

adjustments.text: Severe renal impairment may require dose reduction if toxicity develops; consult the label and interacting-drug recommendations.

pharmacokinetics.text: Lipophilic with extensive tissue distribution and a prolonged terminal elimination phase; food slows absorption without reducing overall extent.

pharmacodynamics.text:
Rifabutin is a rifamycin acting on bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, with activity against susceptible mycobacteria. Cross-resistance with rifampicin is common; rifabutin susceptibility must not be assumed in rifampicin-resistant infection. US prescribing information: microbiology.

In a clinical pharmacokinetic substudy involving patients with HIV and TB receiving intermittent therapy, lower rifabutin AUC0–24 was associated with failure or relapse accompanied by acquired rifamycin resistance. Population and regimen characteristics limit generalisation. Weiner et al., 2005.

Unresolved evidence gap: A universally validated human rifabutin AUC/MIC target was not identified. Exposure associated with failure in a particular cohort should not be treated as a universal therapeutic cutoff or replaced with a rifampicin-derived target.

A Cochrane review of five trials (924 participants; only one trial methodologically adequate) found no significant cure or relapse difference between rifabutin- and rifampicin-containing regimens; people with HIV were under-represented and evidence did not support shortening treatment. This is comparative regimen-outcome evidence, not a validated rifabutin AUC/MIC target and not evidence for rifabutin in rifampicin-resistant TB. PMC-RIFABUTIN-COCHRANE-2009.

source_inclusion_approval.scope: Approval covers inclusion and citation of the listed references in the antibiotic module; it is not clinical validation or approval for treatment decisions.

safety.text: Uveitis, neutropenia, rash and gastrointestinal intolerance are relevant; body fluids may discolor.

interactions.text: CYP3A inhibitors increase rifabutin exposure; rifabutin induction can reduce companion-drug exposure. Clarithromycin and boosted ART require careful review.

populations.text: Exclude active TB before MAC prophylaxis; pregnancy and pediatric evidence are limited in this label.

administration.text: Capsules may be taken with food for tolerance; do not substitute another rifamycin milligram for milligram.

monitoring.text: Monitor blood counts and ocular symptoms; eye pain or blurred vision requires prompt evaluation.

stewardship.text: A prophylactic label must not be used to justify rifamycin monotherapy in unrecognized active tuberculosis.

records.name: Rifampicin
forms: Oral capsules; oral programme FDCs require exact component identities

overview.text: Rifampicin, called rifampin in US labeling, is a central TB drug with major interaction potential.

mechanism.text: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, blocking RNA synthesis.

spectrum.text: Susceptible M. tuberculosis; the label also addresses meningococcal carriage. Other in-vitro activity does not establish routine indications.

indications.text: TB combinations; rifampicin also forms part of Indian leprosy triple MDT.

dosing.text: India / NTEP context: adult DS-TB uses daily HRZE for 2 months followed by HRE for 4 months, with weight-band FDCs; the national workflow lists rifampicin 10 mg/kg daily (usual range 8–12 mg/kg). For the NTEP H-mono/poly-resistant TB regimen, the adult weight-band table lists 300 mg (16–29 kg), 450 mg (30–45 kg), 600 mg (46–70 kg), or 750 mg (>70 kg) daily. Leprosy MDT uses a separate schedule.

adjustments.text: An Indian Society of Critical Care Medicine position statement reports that isoniazid and rifampicin do not require dose adjustment in renal failure. This is a general renal statement; severe hepatic disease, interactions, dialysis timing, weight-band formulation and the full NTEP regimen still require specialist review.

pharmacokinetics.text: Food reduces absorption; hepatic deacetylation produces an active metabolite, with biliary elimination and enterohepatic cycling.

pharmacodynamics.text: A systematic review/meta-analysis found low 2-hour post-dose concentrations in a pooled 67% of studied patients for rifampicin; only 3 of 12 studies examining outcomes found an association between low concentration and unsuccessful treatment. The authors noted uncertainty around accepted concentration thresholds. This supports selective specialist TDM in suspected malabsorption, delayed response or unusual risk, but does not establish a universal target or authorize automatic dose escalation. Use the complete NTEP combination regimen and susceptibility results.

safety.text: Hepatotoxicity, severe skin reactions, thrombocytopenia and renal reactions can occur. Orange body-fluid discoloration is expected.

interactions.text: Potent enzyme/transporter induction affects antiretrovirals, anticoagulants, contraceptives, immunosuppressants and many other drugs.

populations.text: Pregnancy and neonatal bleeding risk warrant assessment; hepatic disease increases monitoring needs.

administration.text: Take oral capsules with water, following product instructions on separation from meals and antacids.

monitoring.text: Check medication changes, liver symptoms and relevant blood counts; monitor anticoagulation when interacting therapy is unavoidable.

stewardship.text: Resistance results, indication and full companion regimen must be reviewed before substitution or interrupted treatment is restarted.

records.name: Rifapentine
forms: Oral 150 mg film-coated tablets in inspected US label

overview.text: Long-acting rifamycin used in specific TB-treatment or preventive combinations. Frequency depends on the exact regimen and population.

mechanism.text: Blocks bacterial RNA synthesis through DNA-dependent RNA polymerase inhibition.

spectrum.text: Susceptible M. tuberculosis; rifampicin resistance generally makes use inappropriate without specialist interpretation.

indications.text: US label includes drug-susceptible pulmonary TB and latent-TB treatment with companion drugs; Indian eligibility must be checked separately.

dosing.text: India / NTEP preventive-treatment context: the NTEP/NACO 1HP option for eligible people living with HIV aged ≥13 years is rifapentine 600 mg plus isoniazid 300 mg orally once daily for 28 days, after active TB disease has been ruled out and ART interactions/eligibility have been reviewed. This is preventive treatment, not an active-TB regimen; confirm the latest local NTEP protocol before use.

adjustments.text:
A primary study administered a single 600 mg dose to 15 patients with stable hepatic dysfunction. Overall AUC was similar between impairment groups and approximately 19–25% higher than historical healthy-volunteer values. Although the authors suggested no adjustment was necessary, this does not validate every repeated-dose regimen. Keung et al., 1998.

The WHO-prequalified Macleods 300 mg tablet SmPC requires careful monitoring in chronic liver disease and lists acute liver disease, icterus and severe hepatic impairment as contraindications. It recommends baseline/periodic liver enzymes and monthly clinical monitoring. Renal-impairment PK data and a numerical renal adjustment formula are absent. This is WHO-prequalification product information, not confirmation of an Indian marketing permission. Macleods WHOPAR, §§4.2–4.4 and 5.2.

A population-PK analysis of latent-TB datasets identified food, HIV status and autoinduction as exposure covariates, but it did not supply renal-impairment or dialysis PK data. These exposure differences do not answer the organ-adjustment question and should not be converted into a new regimen outside applicable guidance. PMC population-PK analysis.

Unresolved evidence gap: a validated renal/dialysis adjustment algorithm and robust repeated-dose evidence in significant hepatic disease remain unavailable. Apply the relevant product restrictions rather than replacing them with the older single-dose study’s conclusion.

source_inclusion_approval.scope: Approval covers inclusion and citation of the listed references in the antibiotic module; it is not clinical validation or approval for treatment decisions.

pharmacokinetics.text: Highly protein bound; an active desacetyl metabolite contributes to prolonged exposure.

pharmacodynamics.text: Two phase II pulmonary-TB studies found rifapentine AUC0–24 exposure related to culture conversion; a modeled AUC threshold was specific to those regimens, food conditions, trial populations and assays. Do not transfer the trial target to India’s weekly 3HP preventive regimen or use it for automatic dose escalation.

safety.text: Hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity, severe cutaneous reactions and hematologic reactions are important precautions.

interactions.text: Induces CYP3A4 and CYP2C8/9; hormonal contraceptives and many antiretrovirals may lose effectiveness.

populations.text: Pediatric weight bands and pregnancy risk require the specific programme protocol; US label age limits vary by indication.

administration.text: Take with meals; label permits crushing tablets into a small quantity of semisolid food consumed immediately.

monitoring.text: Assess hepatic symptoms, rash, adherence and medication interactions throughout the planned course.

stewardship.text: Exclude active TB before preventive therapy and use the prescribed effective combination without improvised missed-dose substitutions.

overview.text: Systemic antibacterial medicine; exact salts, route and formulation must be confirmed against the Indian product. [TB regimen note below is indication-specific.]

mechanism.text: Aminoglycoside; binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and inhibits bacterial protein synthesis.

spectrum.text: Susceptibility is organism- and resistance-specific. For TB, use molecular/phenotypic drug-susceptibility results and NTEP regimen criteria; do not infer activity from class alone.

indications.text: The 2023 NTEP/ICMR workflow mentions streptomycin only in selected situations such as TB meningitis or when a first-line medicine must be replaced because of an adverse reaction. It is not listed as a routine current NTEP DR-TB regimen component in the 2025 guideline reviewed.

dosing.text: India / NTEP 2023 workflow: 15 mg/kg IM once daily (usual range 15–20 mg/kg) in selected TB situations only. This historical/special-case workflow entry is not routine DS-TB or DR-TB dosing; confirm current specialist guidance and maximum dose before use.

adjustments.text: Adjust dose/interval to renal function using the exact product protocol; the label notes accumulation with renal impairment.

pharmacokinetics.text: Poor oral absorption; IM administration produces systemic concentrations; predominantly renal elimination.

pharmacodynamics.text: Concentration/exposure relative to organism MIC is relevant to antibacterial activity; no individual TB dose calculator or validated bedside exposure target is supplied here.

safety.text: Nephrotoxicity, irreversible auditory/vestibular ototoxicity, neuromuscular blockade and hypersensitivity.

interactions.text: Additive renal/ear toxicity with other nephrotoxic or ototoxic agents; neuromuscular blockers can increase paralysis risk.

populations.text: Avoid in pregnancy unless no safer effective alternative; older adults and renal/hearing impairment need close specialist oversight.

monitoring.text: Renal function, hearing/vestibular symptoms and serum levels when required by protocol; check pregnancy and neuromuscular risks.

stewardship.text: For TB, use only in a complete susceptibility-guided regimen under NTEP/specialist oversight; never use as monotherapy. For other infections, follow current Indian syndrome guidance, cultures and susceptibility results.

records.name: Terizidone
forms: Oral 250 mg hard capsules; WHO-prequalified presentation

overview.text: Oral second-line TB drug related to cycloserine. Older product instructions and updated WHO PK guidance should be distinguished.

mechanism.text: Activity is mediated by cycloserine, inhibiting bacterial cell-wall synthesis.

spectrum.text: Susceptible M. tuberculosis; appropriate companion drugs are needed to prevent resistance.

indications.text: Combination treatment when first-line medicines cannot be used because of resistance or intolerance.

dosing.text:
Adult dosing is 10–15 mg/kg/day PO, maximum 1 g/day, as part of a multidrug TB regimen. WHO TB operational handbook, 2025.

MSF specifies 7.5–10 mg/kg twice daily for children weighing <30 kg, or 15–20 mg/kg once daily if tolerated. Adults and children weighing ≥30 kg receive 5–7.5 mg/kg twice daily, or 10–15 mg/kg once daily if tolerated. The maximum is 1 g/day. Apply the programme’s weight-band table and renal-impairment recommendations. Neuropsychiatric toxicity and tolerability may constrain dosing. MSF Tuberculosis, Appendix 10.

adjustments.text: Renally eliminated active drug requires reduced dosing in renal failure; dialysis timing and specialist monitoring matter.

pharmacokinetics.text: WHO 2025 notes suggest presystemic hydrolysis to cycloserine; parent terizidone is not measurable in plasma using current evidence.

pharmacodynamics.text:
Terizidone provides cycloserine exposure. Cycloserine inhibits enzymes involved in mycobacterial peptidoglycan synthesis. A primary population-PK study in 132 patients used hollow-fibre-derived time-above-MIC targets of approximately 30% for 1-log kill, 64% for 80% of maximal kill, and 100% for suppression of acquired resistance. These remain experimental cycloserine targets. Chirehwa et al., 2020.

A 2026 external model-evaluation study supports estimating cycloserine exposure after terizidone but does not establish a new clinical efficacy threshold. Primary CSF research also identifies uncertainty when extrapolating targets to TB meningitis. Behrens et al., 2026; primary CSF penetration study.

A clinical TDM review repeats the proposed %T>MIC target but notes that higher modeled doses may be poorly tolerated; this reinforces that target attainment alone does not establish a clinically acceptable regimen. It describes TDM as potentially useful in selected complicated MDR-TB cases, not as a universal validated efficacy target. PMC TDM review.

Unresolved evidence gap: a universally validated human terizidone efficacy target remains unavailable. Model-derived exposure estimates and safety-oriented concentration ranges should not be presented as validated efficacy thresholds.

A systematic PK/PD review found no published clinical cycloserine PK/PD studies at the time of its search; its efficacy targets came from a hollow-fiber model and simulations. A later 132-person terizidone study likewise states that human PD indices associated with efficacy are lacking and uses experimental T>MIC targets for simulations. These data support the model-based discussion above but do not validate a clinical efficacy threshold. PMC-CYCLOSERINE-PKPD-SR-2018; PMC-TERIZIDONE-HEPATIC-PK-2019.

source_inclusion_approval.scope: Approval covers inclusion and citation of the listed references in the antibiotic module; it is not clinical validation or approval for treatment decisions.

safety.text: Neuropsychiatric toxicity and seizures are major risks; renal accumulation can worsen them.

interactions.text: Alcohol and other neurotoxic TB medicines require review; do not assume terizidone avoids cycloserine-related toxicity.

populations.text: Pregnancy/lactation and children require expert risk assessment and an appropriate formulation; pyridoxine is important.

administration.text: Follow current formulation instructions; WHO 2025 guidance permits administration irrespective of meals, differing from the older WHOPAR preference.

monitoring.text: Assess renal function, mood, neurological symptoms and, where feasible, active-metabolite concentrations.

stewardship.text: Not a milligram-for-milligram automatic replacement for cycloserine. Obtain specialist agreement on the complete regimen and safety plan.

records.name: Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole)
forms: Oral tablets/suspension; IV formulation; verify the trimethoprim:sulfamethoxazole strength ratio

overview.text: Fixed antibacterial combination; strength is expressed as two components and must be preserved.

mechanism.text: Sequential inhibition of bacterial folate synthesis by sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim.

spectrum.text: Selected susceptible urinary, respiratory and other organisms; resistance is common and Pneumocystis use is a distinct indication.

indications.text: NCDC includes co-trimoxazole in selected Indian enteric-fever, urinary and opportunistic-infection pathways; match the regimen to the indication.

dosing.text:
Weight-based doses must specify the trimethoprim component. One double-strength tablet contains trimethoprim 160 mg plus sulfamethoxazole 800 mg. Adult labelled UTI dosing is one double-strength tablet every 12 hours, with duration selected according to the UTI syndrome and applicable guidance. For labelled paediatric UTI or otitis indications in children aged ≥2 months, administer trimethoprim 8 mg/kg/day plus sulfamethoxazole 40 mg/kg/day, divided every 12 hours. US prescribing information.

For Pneumocystis pneumonia in adults/adolescents with HIV, administer trimethoprim 15–20 mg/kg/day plus sulfamethoxazole 75–100 mg/kg/day. Moderate-to-severe disease generally requires IV administration divided every 6–8 hours; oral treatment is appropriate for selected milder disease or step-down. Recommended duration is 21 days. Preferred prophylaxis includes one double-strength or one single-strength tablet daily. NIH Pneumocystis guideline.

adjustments.text: Renal dose changes depend on creatinine clearance; severe impairment and dialysis require the exact label/protocol.

pharmacokinetics.text: Both components are orally absorbed and renally eliminated; trimethoprim can raise serum creatinine by inhibiting tubular secretion.

pharmacodynamics.text: Sequential pathway blockade can produce enhanced antibacterial activity; clinical exposure targets are indication-specific.

safety.text: Severe cutaneous reactions, marrow suppression, hyperkalemia, renal effects, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency and anaphylaxis are important.

interactions.text: Major interactions include warfarin, methotrexate, phenytoin, sulfonylureas and potassium-raising drugs; check current label.

populations.text: Contraindications/restrictions include young infants and late pregnancy in the cited label; assess folate status, G6PD and comorbidity.

administration.text: Use the prescribed component strength; maintain hydration when appropriate and follow product-specific administration directions.

monitoring.text: CBC, renal function, potassium, rash/mucosal symptoms and INR or drug levels when interacting medicines are present.

stewardship.text: Culture-directed use and de-escalation matter; do not infer susceptibility from a syndrome or historical local resistance estimate.

records.name: Vancomycin
forms: IV infusion for systemic infection; oral capsules/solution for intestinal lumen indications; route matters

overview.text: Glycopeptide; IV and oral routes have different clinical uses because oral absorption is poor.

mechanism.text: Binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini and blocks bacterial cell-wall synthesis.

spectrum.text: Susceptible Gram-positive organisms including MRSA; no useful Gram-negative activity.

indications.text: NCDC includes IV vancomycin in selected MRSA-risk pathways; oral therapy is reserved for appropriate intestinal infection protocols.

dosing.text:
For serious invasive MRSA infection in adults with normal renal function, an initial dose of 15–20 mg/kg IV every 8–12 hours using actual body weight is individualised to achieve AUC24 400–600 mg·h/L, assuming a broth-microdilution MIC of 1 mg/L. Target exposure should be achieved within 24–48 hours. Loading doses, obesity and renal replacement therapy require specific dosing pathways. Trough-only targeting of 15–20 mg/L is no longer recommended for this indication. Vancomycin consensus guideline.

For an initial nonfulminant adult C. difficile infection when vancomycin is selected, administer 125 mg PO four times daily for 10 days. Fulminant disease requires 500 mg PO or by nasogastric tube four times daily, with metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours, particularly when ileus is present; ileus may also require rectal vancomycin under specialist guidance. Oral and IV vancomycin serve different indications. IDSA/SHEA CDI guideline.

adjustments.text: Renal clearance drives maintenance exposure; dialysis and rapidly changing kidney function require protocol-specific handling.

pharmacokinetics.text: Poorly absorbed orally; IV distribution and clearance vary with renal function and critical illness.

pharmacodynamics.text: For serious MRSA infection, AUC/MIC-guided exposure is preferred by contemporary monitoring guidance; do not substitute a universal trough target.

safety.text: Infusion reactions, nephrotoxicity, neutropenia and rare ototoxicity; risk increases with exposure and interacting nephrotoxins.

interactions.text: Review other nephrotoxins and concurrent agents affecting renal function; exact interaction assessment depends on patient therapy.

populations.text: Pregnancy and neonatal/pediatric use require population-specific assessment and monitoring.

administration.text: Administer IV only after appropriate dilution and at a controlled rate; oral therapy does not treat systemic infection.

monitoring.text: Renal function and drug exposure per local protocol; monitor infusion reaction, CBC during prolonged therapy and clinical response.

stewardship.text: Use when resistant Gram-positive coverage is justified; stop or narrow when cultures and clinical review permit.
